result.description: Declassified and Approved For Release 2012/05/10 :CIA-RDP90-009658000605410008-1 ~~? ,. ~_- JOI~~ R~ES~ WASHINGTON TIMES 12 June 195 i What the s y cases should teach us n the- Old Testament, Joshua, who "sent out two men to spy secretly" (Joshua 2:1) was the first recorded case officer; however it was Sun Tsu in 5th cen- tury B.C. China who provided the first written guidelines for espi- onage. Defectors from .the intelligence services of the Soviet Union and its Warsaw Pact and Cuban surrogates say that Sun Tsu's The Art of War is required reading for every upwardly mobile spy master. result.title: Donald Hartung Trial Day 3 - Spc Agt Matt Infinger - FDLE, Spc Agt Christopher Williams, Brad Gordon
result.creator: Law&Crime Network
result.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. result.description: Former Equifax CEO Richard Smith testified before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee on his former employer's response to a data breach that left more than 140 million consumers with their personal financial information at risk of theft. result.title: Deposition of STEVEN RICHARD SMITH, M.D., February 11, 1999, ACTON v. R.J. REYNOLDS TOBACCO CO.
result.description: Depositions and Trial Testimony (DATTA); deposition; the defendants' expert witness, a physician specializing in preventive medicine, was deposed by the plaintiffs. he explained that he heads his own corporation, which provides occupational, environmental and preventive medical services to a variety of patients and clients. he indicated that he evaluates workers who seek medical services and determine whether the medical problems are related to occupational injury, illness or disease caused by exposures as work. he performs diagnostic workups, makes diagnoses and provides treatment. he said the most common diseases involve environmental exposures that lead to pulmonary problems, neurological disorders, chemical sensitivities or allergies. the witness said that he had been asked to review mr. acton's medical records and determine whether his small-cell lung cancer was related to secondhand smoke. he mentioned some of the environmental tobacco smoke literature that he reviewed in preparation for the deposition. the witness explained why he did not agree with mr. acton's diagnosis of small-cell lung cancer. he characterized the likelihood of small-cell lung cancer as "so remote as to be not even worthy of entertaining it." he said that even if mr. acton had small-cell lung cancer, it was not caused by secondhand smoke.

result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Wilmington City Council Regular Meeting – March 4, 2025 The Wilmington City Council held its regular meeting on March 4, 2025, at 6:30 PM in City Hall. The meeting included presentations, public comments, public hearings, ordinances, resolutions, and a closed session. Key actions included approving a 5–2 rezoning for a commercial parking lot, unanimously supporting a substitute resolution urging NCDOT to explore all practical alternatives for the Cape Fear Memorial Bridge replacement, and accepting over $2.4 million in federal funding for a multi-use path. ### Presentations - Mayor Saffo read and presented a Proclamation naming March 2025 as Women’s History Month, accepted by Sheila Evans, Chair of the Wilmington/New Hanover County Commission for Women. - David Ingram (Sustainability Manager) and Richard Smith (Clean Energy Advisory Committee Chair) presented the annual report. Smith highlighted 2024 accomplishments: energy efficiency upgrades at police and fire headquarters (reducing energy usage intensity), LED retrofits, recommendations for a fleet EV transition study, adoption of a Sustainable Municipal Building Policy, and contributions to C-PACE. 2025 goals include expanding the EV pilot project (currently two Nissan Leafs at public works), pursuing SOLSMART Silver/Gold accreditation, and enhanced communication. Smith noted two current committee vacancies. ### Consent Calendar - **C1–C3** approved unanimously (7-0): - Approval of minutes from January 31, February 4, February 17, and February 18, 2025 council meetings. - Resolution authorizing a $332,347 golf cart lease agreement with Club Car, LLC for the Wilmington Municipal Golf Course. - Resolution authorizing retirement of Police Canine Officer Jacco and transfer to Corporal David Garriques. Mayor Saffo thanked K-9 Jacco for his service. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Cynthia Gierer** (tenant at Arboretum West Apartments) described unresolved mold, pest, and plumbing issues after a pipe burst; she said code enforcement directed her to legal aid rather than taking action. - **Michael O’Leary** (resident in Brooklyn Arts District) opposed the social district pilot, citing noise, parking, public intoxication, and DUI risks. He provided statistics: North Carolina ranks third nationally in alcohol-related fatalities, with 345 fatal crashes and 12,146 alcohol-related crashes in 2023; estimated $10 billion annual cost of alcohol abuse in NC. He referenced a European study finding 19% of festival attendees drive home intoxicated. - **Alex White** (owner of Pizzeria Don Luca) supported the social district pilot, reporting that the three Saturdays of the program were the three busiest days in his shop’s history; sales doubled February 2024 totals, employee tips tripled, and he observed no negative incidents. He expressed willingness to address parking concerns. - **Elizabeth O’Donnell** (resident on South 2nd Street) urged council not to support a 135-foot fixed-span bridge, which she said would destroy her historic home and neighborhood. She supported the 100-foot option, noting reduced bridge openings (approximately 67 for sailboats in the past year) and lack of dredging plans north of the bridge. - **Elizabeth Wright** (resident on South 2nd Street) argued the 100-foot option is fiscally responsible and less disruptive. She cited declining large-vessel use north of the bridge, and warned that a 135-foot bridge could threaten federal funding and lead to tolls. She highlighted potential impacts to Davis Funeral Home and other historic businesses. - **Susan Bullock** (resident, Wrightsville Beach Chamber chair) requested postponement of the proposed U-5710 flyover bridge at Eastwood Road and Military Cutoff, suggesting the $85 million be reallocated. She described expected traffic congestion from overlapping construction projects. ### Public Hearings - **PH1 – Special Use Permit at 5651 Greenville Loop Road:** Unanimously continued (7-0) to June 17, 2025 meeting. - **PH2 – C-PACE Program:** Resolution authorizing City participation passed unanimously (7-0). David Ingram noted no budgetary impact and that New Hanover County adopted the program on February 17, 2025. - **PH3 – Rezoning at 4717 College Acres Drive** (R-5(CD) to CB(CD) for commercial parking lot): Staff recommended denial, citing inconsistency with the Comprehensive Plan; Planning Board recommended approval (5-2). After testimony from applicant Cindee Wolfe and property manager Grace Sneed (who presented 223 signatures in favor), council approved the rezoning on a 5-2 vote (Councilmembers Joyner and Andrews voted no). Second reading waived unanimously. - **PH4 – Rezoning at 5601 Oleander Drive** (CB to RB(CD) for commercial recreation center): Unanimously approved (7-0). Applicant John Reese described a 40,816 sq. ft. facility with arcade, bowling (10 lanes traditional, 8 duckpin), axe throwing, pickleball courts, restaurant, and bar. The applicant will install a traffic light at no cost to the city. Second reading waived. - **PH5 – Rezoning at 102 & 104 Meares Street** (R-3 to UMX): Unanimously approved (7-0). Applicant Christian Cardamone emphasized alignment with Southside Small Area Plan and potential for mixed-use infill. Second reading waived. - **PH6 – Rezoning at 6624 & 6710 Market Street** (R-15 to RB): Unanimously approved (7-0). Staff said the rezoning is consistent with surrounding commercial uses. Second reading waived. ### Discussion Items - **Clean Energy Advisory Committee Annual Report** (presented earlier). No separate discussion beyond presentation. - **Cape Fear Memorial Bridge Resolution:** Councilmember Andrews introduced a substitute resolution supporting a 100-foot fixed-span replacement. After extensive debate, the motion lacked a second. Mayor Saffo presented a substitute resolution urging NCDOT, US Coast Guard, and US Army Corps of Engineers to explore all practical alternatives to prevent negative impacts to homes, businesses, and historic structures. New Deputy Chief of Mission Arthur Hughes arrived at post 7 August. Mr Hughes paid a 2-hour familiarization visit to the bureau on the 27th. The bureau chief gave the new DCM a tour of the premises and introduced him to bureau personnel. 2. The bureau also proposed that the embassy examine the current system of disseminating FBIS material to embassy consumers. Bowart and Richard Sutton Editor's note: Walter Bowart's Opera- tion Mind Control caused a furor in the United States intelligence commun- ity when it was first published in 1975. Bowart's research on the sub- ject of. government agency involve- ment in dangerous and often life- threatening human experimentation on unwitting citizens paved the way for a new era in exposure of such unconstitutional' practices. As a re- sult, many such experiments were halted, and the responsible govern- ment agencies were forced to release information which had previously been hidden from the general public. Bowart continued his research into the horrifying, mind-crippling effects of government exploitation of its own citizens in mind control experimenta- tion. What he uncovered is more incredible than any science fiction novel. In the as-yet unpublished manu- script, The Invisible Third World War, Bowart and co-author Richard Sut- ton reveal that the world is already locked in deadly, invisible warfare, fighting for the ultimate prize - the mind of man. When the first atomic bomb was detonated at Alamogordo, New Mex- ico, in 1944, the warriors of the mod- ern world experienced a flath,of in- sight that changed the nature of war forever. The men who built the bomb realized that civilian populations were now unavoidable targets, and that conventional war had now become a dangerous trigger which could cata- lyze an earth-destroying retaliation with nuclear weapons. Such old-fashioned methods of war- fare as gunpowder, employed by revo- lutionaries fighting protracted con- flicts, were suddenly perceived as potential threats which could ignite the nuclear holocaust. The only safe way to wage war, the warriors realized, was to wage it silently. Invisible Warfare - or IW, as it came to be known - became a necessity. By the end of World War II, IW research had begun in earnest, and in the ensuing decades, modern war- riors developed a number of insidious methods of subduing enemy popula- tions without their ever knowing that a war had even begun. Secret, invisible weapons now pose a more ominous threat to life than even thermonuclear holocaust. Not only have these weapons been devel- oped without the knowledge of their intended victims, but, worse, they cannot even be detected at the very moment they are murdering or rob- otizing civilian populations. Only if the veil of secrecy is lifted will the free people of the world have any hope of surviving long enough to liberate themselves from the bleak, unlivable future promised by the tech- nology of Invisible War. Chemical and Biological Warfare The Secret Plagues Governments do experiment on their own citizens. In the Soviet Union, the victims never get a chance to talk about it. The signal's strength was rated at 500,000 watts - 10times the Federal Communica- tions Commission (FCC) radio li- censed limit. The signal extended as far away as the next town, Corvallis. After receiving 150 documented complaints about the signal, Gover- nor Bob Straub, Senator Mark Hat- field, and Congressman Jim Weaver were prompted to demand an Envi- ronmental Protection Agency (EPA) investigation. A data analysis by the State Health Department's Radiation Control Sec- tion determined that there was "prob- able cause" linking the complaints to the strange frequency. Said Clifford Shrock, a Textronix, Inc. radio frequency analyst who had written electronics manuals for the CIA and the National Security Agency (NSA), "I was surprised. I'd ~er seen anything like it before." Reactions to the story flooded in from around the world. Calls came in from people who had similar stories to tell about their own distant areas. Several calls came in from technicians offering their hypotheses about the signal, suggesting a possible link to secret weapons radiation. The people of Eugene began to learn about Electromagnetic Radia- tion (EMR) biohazards in a hurry. No one, however, could get to the bottom of Eugene's problem. The FCC's Enforcement Division assistant chief, Richard Smith, flatly attributed the frequency to a naval transmitter at Dixon, California, nicknamed the "Dixon Duck." Van Ert and others disputed this conclusion. The Navy denied that the Dixon Duck was responsible. When the EPA technicians finally arrived, however, they proclaimed that the mysterious signal did not exist at all. Van Ert, Shrock and others who had felt the signal and measured it strongly disagreed with them. But the EPA investigators held a press conference at which they dis- credited the reports of the strange Eugene Signal and promptly returned to their Las Vegas headquarters, where they refused to speak to reporters. After this, the investigation folded altogether. The Eugene Signal remains an offi- cial mystery. Although the people of Eugene didn't know it, both the U.S. and Soviet military had been working for years to perfect the use of electro- magnetic frequencies as lethal psy- chological weapons. Similar symptoms reported in such places as Timmons and Kirkland Lake in Canada were traced to a notorious Soviet radio broadcast dubbed by ama- teur radio operators "the woodpecker." result.description: This is a repost of a discussion I had on The Meaning Code YouTube channel and podcast with Karen Wong, Dr. Richard Smith and Dr. Wolfgang Smith. The majority of this discussion was about bringing my and Wolfgang's work together. result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Board of Port Wardens Meeting – December 11, 2025 The Board of Port Wardens of Ocean City, Maryland, met on December 11, 2025, at 2:00 PM in City Hall Council Chambers. The meeting addressed the approval of previous minutes, 12 permit cases (5 minor, 7 major), and a public hearing on proposed amendments to Chapter 106 (Waterways) of the Town Code. All permit cases were approved unanimously, often with staff-recommended conditions. The code revision discussion centered on updating marine construction standards and clarifying the board’s authority to grant exceptions. ### Consent Calendar - **Minutes Approval:** The board unanimously approved the minutes from the October 9, 2025 meeting (motion by Rich, second by Melvin; voice vote all in favor). ### Minor Cases (Unanimously Approved) Each minor case was presented with staff recommendations citing compliance with minimum Board of Port Wardens (BOPW) specifications. No letters of objection were received. The board voted 7-0 (all members present) to approve each application per staff recommendations. - **PW 25-087** – 611 Gulf Stream Drive (Stephen Folckemmer): Install five 12"×20' batter piles (5'11" channelward max). - **PW 25-088** – 14202 Laurel Avenue (Kathleen Frock): Replace existing 5'×30' dock with a 3.5'×46' dock and repair ±46' of timber bulkhead via vinyl replacement (5' channelward max). - **PW 25-089** – 315 N Heron Gull Court (Richard Smith, Jr.): Replace bulkhead pile system with ten 12"×20' piles, tie rods, and anchors. - **PW 25-090** – 5301 Coastal Highway (Candy Kitchen, LLC): Install ±310' of replacement vinyl bulkhead using a batter pile system (18" channelward max). - **PW 25-095** – 136 Old Landing Road (Anna Smigocki): Remove existing platform, install 60' of replacement vinyl bulkhead, and a new 5'×16' recessed dock (18" channelward max). Staff noted 43.5' of navigable waterway will remain. ### Major Cases (Unanimously Approved with One Exception) All major cases also had no letters of objection and were approved by voice vote. One case required a board exception to the 20% rule. - **PW 25-091** – 205 Somerset Street (White Marlin Marina): Install five mooring piles at end of existing T-pier (174' channelward). Board discussed that these are bumper piles for commercial marina; no objection. - **PW 25-092** – 614 94th Street (Glenn Cantagallo): Install one 12'8"×12'8" floating dock (19' channelward). Staff noted the request exceeds the allowable 20% rule: 20% of 90' waterway width = 18', but the pier already extends 19'. The board granted an exception and approved the application (motion by Joe, second by Rich). The exception allows the work to proceed at 19' channelward. - **PW 25-093** – 411 Bayshore Drive, Unit 302 (Bayshore OC, LLC): Install one jet ski lift with piling (8'2" channelward max). - **PW 25-094** – 609 Bayshore Drive, Unit 32 (Edward Lee): Extend existing 32' pier by 18' to 50' total, install one boat lift with pilings (50' channelward max, open water). - **PW 25-096** – 107 Convention Center Drive (Thunder Island CM): Install 440 linear feet of replacement vinyl bulkhead (18" channelward), relocate 15 finger piers (12'6" channelward max). Board noted 48 mooring piles at the slip front will also move 18" channelward. - **PW 25-097** – 1510 Shad Row (Frederick C. Rummage, Jr.): Install 50' of replacement vinyl bulkhead (18" channelward), one boat lift and one PWC/kayak lift (13' channelward max). Existing pier/platform will be removed. ### Code Revision – Public Hearing and Board Deliberation The board held a public hearing on a proposed ordinance amending Chapter 106 (Waterways), including updated vinyl bulkhead, riprap, pier, and boat lift standards. Planning Director George Bandler reviewed changes: removal of obsolete definitions (e.g., “designated authority”), increased fines for violations (from $1,000 to $5,000 per state authority), addition of condominium/HOA notice requirements, removal of timber bulkhead standards, alignment of building permit expiration (180 days) and marine contractor licensing requirements. The updated marine construction standards were developed in collaboration with Public Works and Vista Design, based on Worcester County standards and reviewed by a bulkhead contractor. Board member comments: - Suggested adding “littoral rights” to the definitional section alongside “riparian rights,” as most of Ocean City’s bayfront involves littoral (tidal) rights (noted by board member). The board and staff agreed to incorporate that change. - Discussed the need for clear authority to grant exceptions to the 20% rule for existing structures that predate the new code. After debate, the board decided to have staff draft language that explicitly allows the board to grant exceptions on a case-by-case basis, rather than codifying specific scenarios. The draft will be circulated via email before the next meeting. - The 200 square-foot maximum for parallel structures and the four-mooring-pile limit were preserved, with commercial exceptions to be handled through board discretion. The public hearing was closed by unanimous vote (motion by Rich, second by Melvin). ### Key Outcomes - **Permit Cases:** All 12 permit applications (PW 25-087 through PW 25-097) were approved unanimously, with PW 25-092 receiving a board exception to allow a 19' channelward extension (1' over the 20% rule). - **Code Revision:** The board will receive revised draft language from staff (including “littoral rights” and exception authority) for review prior to the January 8, 2026 meeting. A favorable recommendation to the City Council is anticipated after that meeting, with a work session scheduled for January 18, 2026 and a second reading on February 17, 2026. - **Next Meeting:** The next regular Board of Port Wardens meeting is scheduled for January 8, 2026 at 2:00 PM.

result.description: # North Kingstown Town Council Meeting — June 22, 2026 The North Kingstown Town Council held a regular meeting on Monday, June 22, 2026, at 7:00 PM in the Town Hall Council Chambers, 80 Boston Neck Road. The council is led by President Gregory A. Mancini, with members Linnea M. Drew, Elizabeth Hill Ross, Dr. Kimberly Ann Page, and Matthew B. McCoy. Notice of the meeting was posted on the Rhode Island Secretary of State's website pursuant to RIGL 42-46-6(c). The docket included special business on the Town Clerk appointment, a 19-item consent calendar (Items 7-25), the Town Manager's report, and new business covering numerous board appointments and a discussion of asphalt odor complaints in the West Davisville area. Record limitations: no meeting minutes were available, and the raw transcript contains no substantive discussion (only the word 'Okay'). As a result, no votes, motions, approvals, or outcomes can be confirmed from the available record. The timestamp associated with the record (2026-06-22 12:00:00 UTC) does not match the 7:00 PM start time listed on the agenda; this summary uses June 22, 2026 as the meeting date, consistent with the agenda. ### Special Business - Item 5: The Town Manager requested the Town Council's Advice and Consent for the appointment of Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk. - Item 6: The Town Manager was scheduled to swear in Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk following the council's action. ### Consent Calendar All items on the Consent Agenda (Items 7-25) were considered routine and were scheduled to be enacted by one motion, with items removed upon a request by a council member or citizen. - Item 7: Approval of minutes from the Special Meeting of March 30, 2026, and the Budget Public Hearings of April 13, 2026. - Item 8: Abatement of uncollectable taxes and fees totaling $128,692.57, including write-offs related to a deceased taxpayer and 2014 personal property, motor vehicle, and rescue accounts. - Item 9: Receipt of a donation of a hand-painted scoreboard to be painted on the side of the Field 1 storage shed at Ryan Park by Caitlin Wotherspoon. - Item 10: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors, LLC (State MPA #308) for an Information Technology Department Zero Trust True Up in the amount of $12,136.61, funded from the Granicus Video Streaming Software Account. - Item 12: Award of a contract extension to CAI Technologies for Assessor's Parcel and Zoning Layer Maintenance and Web Geographic Information System Application, at various prices, funded from the Annual Miscellaneous Software License Account. - Item 13: Award of contract to BEI Holdings, dba Business Electronics, for one Detective Interview Room Recording System for the Police Department in the amount of $14,520.00, funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 14: Approval of a sole source purchase from Motorola Solutions, Inc. of seven portable radios with accessories for the Police Department in the amount of $48,582.87 (State MPA #395), funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 15: Award of a sole source purchase to Advanced Weighing Systems for an upgrade to the Department of Public Works Transfer Station scale computer software in the amount of $10,670.00, funded from the FY2026 Transfer Station Contractual Services Account. - Item 16: Approval of a purchase from Minuteman Security & Life Safety for Department of Senior Services security camera system upgrades and installation of an additional camera in the amount of $15,622.00 (State MPA #419), funded from the Capital Outlay Account. - Item 17: New entertainment license for Cocumscussoc Association, dba Smith's Castle, 55 Richard Smith Drive, for a live concert on the grounds of Smith's Castle on July 19, 2026 (rain date Sunday, August 2, 2026). - Item 25: First reading of an amendment to Section 2-1, entitled 'Competitive Bidding Required.' ### Public Comments & Testimony - The agenda provided a Public Comment period with a three-minute speaking limit, but no public testimony appears in the available transcript. ### Reports - An application was attached from Brian Fielding. - Item 34: Veteran's Memorial Scholarship Fund Committee: two members to July 1, 2027. - Item 35: Wickford Village Design Guidelines Committee: one Alternate Business Property Owner to December 31, 2027. - Item 36: Councilor Beth Hill Ross requested discussion concerning Public Comment. - Item 37: Council President Mancini requested discussion and possible action regarding numerous complaints received by both the Town of North Kingstown and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management about the unacceptable asphalt smell in the West Davisville area. - Item 38: Correspondence. ### Key Outcomes - No decisions, votes, or actions can be confirmed from the available record. result.creator: Law&Crime Network
result.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. result.creator: Law&Crime Network
result.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. result.description: Logbook kept by Josiah C. Long comprised of eight whaling voyages. First voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Shubael Chase, from 24 June 1822 - 27 December 1824 to the Pacific Ocean Contains a long description of the Bounty mutiny and people on Pitcairn Island. The crew also witnessed a total solar eclipse on 26 June 1824. Second voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Edy Coffin, from 7 June 1825 - 16 October 1827 to the Brazil banks, South Pacific Ocean and coast of ChileDuring this voyage the ship saw 125 whales and caught 97. During a stop at the Juan Fernández Islands the ship was able to obtain peaches for the ship. There was one death at sea. Third voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Job C. Clark, from 19 April 1828 - 30 June 1829 to western and southern Atlantic Ocean for sperm and right whales [spelled "write"]. Fourth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Job E. Clark, from 15 November 1829 - 27 January 1833 to the Atlantic Ocean and Pacific Ocean sIn the company of several other vessel at times. Put into port at Rio de Janeiro for repairs. Fifth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 27 June 1833 - 16 November 1836 along Brazil and Chile and the South Pacific OceanDuring the voyage they saw 86 whales and caught 52. They spoke the Charles Carroll's captain Owen Chase who was a survivor of the Essex. Sixth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 1 September 1837 - 28 April 1841 to waters off Brazil, Chile, Peru and the South Pacific OceanThe ship encountered rough weather and could not reach the Azores. During the voyage nine men contracted smallpox. Seveth voyage documents the Richard Mitchell (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 14 October 1843 - 30 September 1847 to Brazil, Galapagos Islands, and the South Pacific OceanIncludes comments on the residents of Pitcairn Islands. It took the ship a month to round Cape Horn. Eighth voyage documents the Charles Carroll (Ship : 1832-1853) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 2 December 1848 - 29 December 1852 along the coast of Peru and the South Pacific Ocean. Voyage began by wrecking the rudder on an oil cask. Includes data on all vessels included in journal.

result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Cranston City Council Finance Committee Budget Hearing - April 16, 2026 The Cranston City Council Finance Committee held a public hearing on the proposed FY2026-2027 budget on April 16, 2026, starting at approximately 7:39 PM and adjourning at 11:49 PM. The meeting focused on the mayor's proposed 7.44% tax levy increase and the financial challenges facing the city, particularly the school department. The committee heard testimony from school committee members, citizens, and representatives from police, fire, schools, and other departments. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **School Committee Vice Chair Anthony Melillo** (33 Harvard Street) presented "myths vs facts," stating that Cranston Public Schools reduced staff by 95 positions over the past four years (not added 100), and that over the last six years the city allocation increased by only about $1 million annually on average, which has not kept pace with rising costs. He emphasized shared responsibility for the budget challenges. - **School Committee Member Catherine Crowley** (Ward 6) explained the school department's structural deficit, noting that the mayor's proposed $1.5 million increase is insufficient. She warned that cuts would lower education quality and deter new teachers. - **School Committee Member Keith Catone** (61 Windsor Road) challenged claims of deficits, stating the school department only recorded a deficit in FY25, while FY24, 23, and 22 had surpluses. He argued that the city budget has been balanced "on the backs of the schools" and that transparency is needed to build public trust. - **Resident Valerie (last name unclear)** stated that taxpayers have "nothing left to give" and urged the council to find budget cuts rather than increase taxes, emphasizing the strain on seniors and families. - **Councilman Steven Steikos** (37 Ferncrest Avenue) observed that school funding increased only 4.3% total from 2024 to 2027, while fire and police funding increased 15.6% and 12.5% respectively. He also noted an $852,000 cash balance in the charter school account and suggested reviewing tax breaks for veterans and elderly. - **Resident Stephen Fryers** (107 Garden Hills Drive) said the budget problem is a "failure in local government" due to over-reliance on one-time federal ARPA funds. He recommended spending cuts and not going above an 8% tax rate effect. - **School Committee Member Anna Madeiris** (21 Bridgeton Court) shared positive stories of student achievements and urged full funding for schools, warning that deteriorating buildings and large class sizes hurt students. - **School Committee Chair Dominic Fusco** (no address provided) noted that Cranston spends $19,950 per student, well below the state average of $22,800. He said the school department has "no choice now but to close schools, increase class sizes, cut programs." - **Local 1363 President Jonathan Francis** (35 Fifth Avenue) defended the fire department, stating that a fifth rescue was added after 40 years and that the department faces 12 vacancies. He said minimum manning of 43 firefighters per shift falls short of the national standard. - **Seventh grader Sally Finkel** (55 Roger Williams Circle) asked to fully fund schools to preserve middle school sports, which she said give students motivation and community. ### Discussion Items #### Police Department Budget (Chief Winquist, Director Strom) - Proposed budget: $33 million. The chief described the budget as "bare bones" and stated that overtime budget of $2.2 million is aligned with historical averages. There are six vacancies; the department had to reduce vehicle purchases from eight to six due to cuts. - Revenue projections were adjusted downward because previous years were overestimated (e.g., police detail car revenues were underperforming). - The department is in contract negotiations; a contingency line item of $700,000 is included for potential contract costs. - Council members questioned gas/oil budget adequacy ($12,500 increase) and the need for more police vehicles given high mileage. The acting director noted oil prices are speculative but assumed the Middle East conflict would not persist. #### Animal Control (Chief Winquist) - The shelter is handling more animals due to economic pressures; budget increase of $10,000 for care. Revenue from impound fees is projected lower due to conservative estimates. - The department uses social media to promote adoptions; average stay is 4-6 weeks. #### Harbor Master - No current harbor master since previous one passed away. The city still collects mooring fees (~$3,500 last year without a harbor master). The council discussed whether to reinstate the position (stipend $3,500) or have police handle duties, but noted the net revenue gain is small. #### School Department Budget (Superintendent Massey, CFO Balducci) - The school department requested $4.2 million new city funding to meet contractual obligations (salary and benefits). The mayor proposed $1.5 million. The state aid increase is estimated at $2 million, but when accounting for a $241,000 reduction in non-public transportation support, net new state money is about $1.8 million. - The school department has a budget savings gap of approximately $3 million (assumes $4 million city ask). If only $1.5 million is provided, the gap grows to $2.5 million. - Cranston Public Schools has cut 95 staff over the last six years and laid off 40 teachers this year; about 12 will likely not be called back. Class sizes are already at contractual limits, and further cuts will increase class sizes and reduce services. - The district spends $19,950 per student, well below the state average. Inflation since 2009 is 56-58%, but city funding only increased 18% over the same period. - Health insurance costs have risen 15% and 10% in the last two years; the district is self-insured and part of a collaborative. A cumulative deficit of $9 million exists, but a new pharmacy contract is expected to generate $4.5 million annually to reduce it. - Charter school impact: $7.2 million in FY25 in tuition and lost state aid. - Discussion of selling former school buildings (Barrows, Waterman) to generate $750,000 one-time for capital needs, but that will not be available in future years. The city solicitor clarified the funds are intended for capital improvements, not tuition. #### Fire Department Budget (Chief, Director Strom) - Proposed overtime budget: $6.3 million (up slightly from FY25 actual of $6.073 million). The chief noted summer overtime is highest and 12 firefighters short, with vacancies due to contractual limits. Fuel costs are a concern due to global prices. - There are 15 firefighters on occupational injury; seven are waiting for state pension board decisions. These injuries increase overtime. - The department had to cut vehicle replacements; two staff vehicles are included. - Council members expressed concern about accuracy of overtime projections given prior years' underfunding. #### Fire Alarm Department - Budget increased for computer maintenance and repairs (licenses increasing). No significant questions. #### Canvassing Department (Director Lima via video) - Proposed operating budget for elections: $215,000, the lowest since 2018. Savings achieved by reducing poll workers (from 315 to 270), cutting poll worker management software (delayed until federal funds available), and benefits from moving the primary to Wednesday (saving ~$25,000). - The department faces increased voter registration transactions (23,822 in 2025) and security needs. Federal election security grant ($50,000) has been fully spent on physical security upgrades. - Potential new state Voting Rights Act may require bilingual ballots, increasing costs. Director Lima noted that federal executive orders could impact mail ballot processing. #### Law Department (Solicitor) - Running under budget at 72.8% year-to-date. No provision for lawsuit settlements; the solicitor recommended budgeting a small contingency. Outside legal services are used for specialized cases and are negotiated at municipal rates (~$200/hour). #### Executive Office (Director Moretti) - Proposing a 0.75% increase (less than 1%), achieved by eliminating one administrative position and consolidating government affairs with communications. Compensation increases for 18 administrative appointees (totaling ~$45,000) were included, but the mayor offered to forego those raises if the council desires, reallocating funds to police vehicles. - The mayor receives a $3,000 annual expense stipend (not monthly). Four city vehicles are assigned to executive staff; fuel and maintenance are charged to the police budget—a legacy accounting practice. Council members questioned this and requested transparency. ### Key Outcomes - No final votes on the budget were taken. The committee will continue deliberations in subsequent hearings, including a planned executive session regarding police contract negotiations. - The council president noted that a 7.44% tax levy increase would require seven out of nine votes (four-fifths) per the city charter, and that nothing is finalized. - The council extended the meeting twice by 30-minute increments to allow full discussion. - Public comment was invited at the meeting's start and end; no online participants spoke. - The meeting adjourned at 11:49 PM.

result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Bourne Planning Board Meeting – August 6, 2026 The Bourne Planning Board held its regular open session at 7 p.m. on August 6, 2026, recorded for live broadcast and televised replay on Bourne TV. The agenda included welcoming the new Building Commissioner, approving the July 23, 2026 meeting minutes, considering a cash bond release for One Katie Marie Drive, and discussing a range of future zoning and infrastructure topics. Note: The raw transcript recites the date as Thursday, August 13th, 2026, but the supplied meeting timestamp is 2026-08-06; this summary uses the supplied date. ### Introduction of New Building Commissioner - Eleanor McKay, the town’s new Building Commissioner, introduced herself. She is an architect with over 35 years of experience and a Bachelor of Architecture from Roger Williams University, licensed since 1997. Her municipal experience includes zoning enforcement in Falmouth, zoning/affordable housing work in Hingham, service on the Duxbury Finance Committee, and work in Harwich. - She expressed enthusiasm for collaborating with the Planning Board and town staff, and described her approach to code enforcement: everyone should play by the same rules, and she prefers to investigate, talk with property owners, and reach resolutions. - Board members welcomed her and discussed the need for follow-through on conditions attached to approvals, including certificate-of-occupancy review. A plan was mentioned for enforcement issues to be routed through Town Planner Jen, with the Commissioner reporting back in about a month. ### Minutes - Motion to approve the July 23, 2026 minutes was made by Chris and seconded by Jim. Board members Steve, Stock, Chris, and the Chair voted yes; Mandy abstained because she was not present. Minutes were approved. ### Bond Release – One Katie Marie Drive (Map 35, Parcel 12) - Staff reported completing a site inspection on August 6, 2026. The parcel, developed as The Shed Place, received site plan review in November 2005, a certificate of occupancy in February 2008, and was recently sold by Ralph Bartlett to a new owner. - Staff found the office, shed display areas, retaining walls, lighting, and signage sufficient. However, several plantings were missing—about four or five—and a weeping willow was missing from the west side; two small dirt piles also need better maintenance. - The cash bond is in Ralph Bartlett’s name and does not transfer with the property, so the new owner is not obligated under the bond. The new property owner was identified in discussion as Pine Harbor. The board voted to release the cash bond plus interest and to send the new property owner a letter of encouragement regarding landscaping and cleanup. ### Future Zoning Changes and Other Business - The Chair said Town Planner Jen would send a preliminary wish list of possible zoning bylaw changes for a future Town Meeting, including cleanup of defunct provisions and larger topics such as the Seasonal Communities Act, tiny homes, ADU regulations, and Chapter 48 / Affordable Homes Act changes. Board members were invited to add suggestions. - The board discussed recent amendments to M.G.L. c. 40A effective July 1, 2026, and the possibility of inviting Town Counsel to brief the Planning Board and ZBA. - Plans were shared to request an update from the Cape Cod Commission on bridge-related planning and to send the Select Board recommendations for incorporation into a state MOU. Board members raised infrastructure considerations for the bridges, including sewer and water piping and a first-responder communications repeater. - Discussion on the Joint Base Cape Cod included the ongoing base master plan update, roughly 200 acres proposed for divestment, the 22,000-acre base, and tours scheduled in August, September, and October. Members discussed potential town interests such as housing, technology park use, solar fields, cemetery space, and regional sewer expansion. A prior multi-town sewage-sharing proposal was recalled as unsuccessful because four municipalities had different approaches. ### Key Outcomes - Approved the July 23, 2026 minutes. - Released the cash bond plus interest for One Katie Marie Drive and directed a letter to the new owner about property upkeep. - Agreed to review the zoning wish list at future meetings and consider requesting presentations from Town Counsel and the Cape Cod Commission. - Reminded the board of the September 8 joint meeting with the Select Board to appoint the Planning Board alternate position; the meeting will be Zoom-only, and five members had confirmed a quorum.

A comprehensive overview of America's vast poetic heritage, Three Centuries of American Poetry features the work of some 150 of our nation's finest writers. From the Revolutionary and Civil Wars to the Romantic Era and the Gilded and Modern Ages, this unrivaled anthology also presents a memorable array of rare ballads, songs, hymns, spirituals, and carols that echo through our nation's history. Highlights include Native American poems, African American writings, and the works of Quakers, colonists, Huguenots, transcendentalists, scholars, slaves, politicians, journalists, and clergymen. These discerning selections demonstrate that the American canon of poetry is as diverse as the nation itself, and constantly evolving as we pass through time. Most important, this collection strongly reflects the peerless styling that mark the American poetic experience as unique. Here, in one distinguished volume, are the many voices of the New World

result.title: Between church and state : religion and public education in a multicultural America
result.creator: Fraser, James W., 1944- author
description: x, 284 pages ; 23 cm

Today, the ongoing controversy about the place—or lack of place—of religion in public schools is a burning issue in the United States. Prayer at football games, creationism in the classroom, the teaching of religion and morals, and public funding for private religious schools are just a few of the subjects over which people are skirmishing. In Between Church and State, historian and pastor James W. Fraser shows that these battles have been going on for as long as there have been public schools and argues there has never been any consensus about what the "separation of church and state" means for American society or about the proper relationship between religion and public education. Looking at the difficult question of how private issues of faith can be reconciled with the very public nature of schooling, Fraser’s classic book paints a complex picture of how a multicultural society struggles to take the deep commitments of people of faith into account—including people of many different faiths and no faith. In this fully updated second edition, Fraser tackles the culture wars, adding fresh material on current battles over public funding for private religious schools. He also addresses the development of the long-simmering evolution-creationism debate and explores the tensions surrounding a discussion of religion and the accommodation of an increasingly religiously diverse American student body. Between Church and State includes new scholarship on the role of Roger Williams and William Penn in developing early American conceptions of religious liberty. It traces the modern expansion of Catholic parochial schools and closely examines the passage of the First Amendment, changes in American Indian tribal education, the place of religion in Booker T. Washington and W. E. B. Du Bois’s debates about African American schooling, and the rapid growth of Jewish day schools among a community previously known for its deep commitment to secular public education. -- Provided by publisher

creator: Swan, Bradford F. (Bradford Fuller) fmo RIBRL

description: Ms. codex
Title taken from ms. slip of covers of volumes 1-3
Dates of publication suggested by JCB Catalogue of manuscript codices

Originally made up of eight volumes, this manuscript Indian and English dictionary consists of four surviving volumes. Based on an extensive compilation process in which terms for various North American Indian languages were collected from different sources. The sources used included A key into the language of America / by Roger Williams, first printed in 1643, with words in the Narragansett language, designated as "RW" in the manuscript, a list of Nanticoke terms labeled as "Nan" and other lists as yet unidentified, labeled as "A", "B", "C", "H", "L", "S", "W", and "Z"

Dictionary entries were written on lined paper and then cut out as individual slips and pasted onto the pages of unrelated printed books in an alphabetical arrangement, forming an attempt at a comprehensive dictionary of Indian and English terms, probably limited to Algonquian languages used in the northeastern United States

Volume 1 has 142 pages and consists of entries Aa to Me; the papers are pasted on the sheets of volume 2 of The history of the wars which arose out of the French Revolution to which is prefixed, a review of the causes of that event / by Alexander Stephens, Philadelphia, 1804. This volume retains its title page, is bound in full contemporary mottled calf and measures 22 cm. tall

Volume 2 has p. 171-359 and consists of entries Me to Wa; the papers are pasted on sheets made up from a German hymnbook. This volume is bound in contemporary full mottled calf and measures 18 cm. tall

Volume 3 has p. 360-421 and consists of entries Wa to Zed, and a supplementary list for entried Ach to Yu, on p. 422-447; the papers are pasted on sheets made up from a German theological text. This volume is bound in contemprary full mottled calf and measures 17 cm. tall
Volumes 1-3 are housed in three cream cloth covered phase boxes with volumes 3 and 4 being housed together; the phase boxes measure 25 cm. tall

result.title: Special Committee on Ways and Means Reviews PPSD FY2027 Budget – May 28, 2026
result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Special Committee on Ways and Means Reviews PPSD FY2027 Budget – May 28, 2026 The Special Committee on Ways and Means, chaired by Miguel Sanchez, met on May 28, 2026, at 5:37 PM. The committee heard a detailed presentation from Providence Public School District (PPSD) leadership on the proposed FY2027 budget, which faces a $1.3 million decline in state aid and uses $3.2 million from reserves. The discussion covered enrollment declines, charter school tuition pressures, staffing reductions, and support for students experiencing homelessness. ### Appointment to Zoning Board - After being moved out of order, the committee approved the appointment of Mr. Scott to a full term on the Zoning Board. Mr. Scott had served as second alternate since 2019 and replaced Chairman Greenfield. The motion passed unanimously on a voice vote. ### Discussion Items - **Budget Overview:** PPSD leadership (Superintendent, Deputy Superintendent, and Chief of Operations) presented the FY2027 budget. Key challenges include declining enrollment (from 23,000 to ~19,000 students), rising fixed costs (transportation, special education tuition, benefits), and a loss of state aid due to fewer students and lower poverty rates. The district has reduced staff by over 500 FTEs since the start of state intervention, including 22 teacher layoffs for the coming year (total of 109 FTE reduction, 4%). - **Revenue:** State aid is projected at $211.3 million, a $1.3 million decline from FY2026. The city contribution is based on a settlement agreement. To balance the budget, the district plans to use $3.2 million from its reserve fund, reducing the reserve from $4.2 million to $1 million. A potential state funding formula change (increasing the success factor from 40% to 43%) could add $4–4.5 million, but the district did not assume that in planning. - **Expenditures:** Transportation costs increased 15% due to a new contract; the district reduced bus runs by four, saving $400,000. Special education tuition rose 8%, though 24 fewer students are placed out-of-district. Custodial contract extension includes a 3.5% annual escalator. The district reduced planned Chromebook purchases (saving $2 million) and eliminated some central office positions, including the grants writer and an MLL manager, through merging roles. - **Staffing and Layoffs:** The 22 teacher layoffs are primarily in areas of declining enrollment (elementary teachers without ESL certification, business education). The district continues to recruit math, special education, and science teachers. As of the meeting, there were fewer than 60 vacancies, down from mid-70s the previous year. Council members expressed concern about messaging around layoffs versus vacancies. - **Charter School Tuition:** Chair Sanchez highlighted that charter school tuition has risen from $21 million in FY2021 to $35.5 million in FY2026, and called this trend “unsustainable.” Several councilors echoed concerns about the fiscal impact of charter expansion on the district, noting that the funding formula does not allow the district to reduce costs proportionally when students leave. The district noted the enrollment loss transition fund softens the blow but is not sufficient. - **Homeless Student Support:** The district serves 133 students experiencing homelessness (7% of enrollment), providing wraparound services, transportation, and supplies. The district is required to transport students even if they temporarily reside outside Providence, costing $1.2 million annually. Academic outcomes for homeless students are significantly lower (e.g., 7% gap in ELA proficiency). Council members asked about data collection and federal grant funding. - **UCAP Program Closure:** The district ended its partnership with UCAP (a middle school program), affecting 42 seventh graders returning to the district. The district created a cohort program at Roger Williams Middle School with additional interventions at a fraction of the previous cost ($1.9 million for UCAP vs. much less for internal services). Only four of the 42 students have IEPs. Councilor Picardo expressed reservations about the transition plan and requested more detailed information. - **Procurement Transition:** Concerns were raised about potential delays in procurement as the district returns to local control. Councilor Davidson’s working group is developing recommendations to maintain efficient procurement while ensuring fiscal oversight. - **Technology and Cybersecurity:** Following a cybersecurity attack last year (no ransom paid), the district implemented new endpoint protection (Falcon) and applied for a grant for employee training. The district also discussed its use of Canvas (LMS) and iReady, noting that iReady is part of a broader Curriculum Associates package and that they monitor the class action lawsuit regarding student data privacy. - **PCTA Facility:** Council members raised concerns about the closure of PCTA for summer recreation programs (impacting 400+ children) due to maintenance; the district expects the facility to be available next summer. Alternative sites (Hope High School) have capacity and cleanliness issues. ### Key Outcomes - The committee voted to **continue items 1–5** (budget items) without a final vote, pending final state revenue numbers and further discussion at the school board. The budget will return for final approval in September. - The appointment to the Zoning Board was **approved unanimously**. - The meeting was **adjourned** after a motion by Councilor Davidson, seconded by Councilor Graves. - The committee plans further meetings to deepen partnership with PPSD as it returns to local control.

result.title: Theresa El Amin's Message To SURJ Providence
result.creator: Andrew Stewart
result.description: Interview of Theresa El-Amin by Andrew Stewart in September 2021. Theresa El-Amin is a movement elder in the most literal sense of the word. A veteran of the Civil Rights movement and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC ) who took marching orders from Kwame Ture/Stokley Carmichael, she spent a few years as an organizer in Providence at Rhode Island Jobs with Justice. On September 11, 2021, she came back to Providence. A mutual friend of ours invited me to a small, intimate conversation with a select few other participants. In a wide-ranging conversation, loaded with both wisdom and practical advice, she put on no pretense of importance despite certainly being entitled to that, something demonstrated by an important column written for Against the Current by our mutual friend and comrade Paul Buhle some years ago , who wrote: El-Amin, born in Georgia in 1948, daughter of a nurse and union shop steward, went to Tuskegee, got involved in SNCC, went through Freedom Summer and the inevitable assault by the FBI, then took a job at the local telephone company when the SNCC office closed. There El-Amin became a shop steward herself, learned about the familiar struggle against racism (by the company and the union alike) and the emerging struggle over the changing workplace, notably the assorted dangers of long hours at the VDT. This led her to 9 to 5 and the Coalition of Labor Union Women (CLUW), and a move to Cleveland, organizing clerical workers (including a big victory at the Cleveland Public Library). By the time she reached Providence, El-Amin had also become a regular at Labor Notes meetings, an ardent supporter of the South African labor federation COSATU and of Black Workers for Justice back at home. She had organized for SEIU, 1199, and joined the Board of DARE as it began to gain prominence. Instead, repeatedly she called on me and other participants in the discussion by name, injecting a dimension that made this one of the most privileged events I have ever attended. The next day, we sat down for a conversation at a bench in the Roger Williams National Park on North Main Street. There was something strikingly important about this location. Williams, who remains a hero to liberals in Rhode Island, in fact was responsible for selling POWs of the Pequot War into slavery in the Caribbean, commencing the chattel bond slave trade in the British North American colonies. We discussed the role that SURJ plays in the struggle to dismantle systemic white supremacy and racism, contemporary politics, and other matters. It will remain one of the most important interviews that I have ever conducted. Regrettably, it cuts off mid-sentence due to the interruption of a phone call on my iPhone recorder. Afterwards, Theresa asked me to drive her around for some errands, meaning there might be some ideas that are dropped without further discussion. Nevertheless, she told me that we will remain comrades (we ended up being able to gossip about a few mutual friends in the radical community, making for some great conversation). That was the greatest gift of all.

result.creator: TewksburyTV
result.description: The Amistad Trials is the first civil rights trial in American history. The issue of slavery versus freedom rears its ugly head in this American court battle, more than two decades before the Civil War explodes in 1861. The case pits the American government against the Spanish government, the President against his own Secretary of State, our executive branch versus the judicial branch, and abolitionists against slave traders. It even prompted a former President to appear before the Supreme Court to condemn the policies of a present administration. Led by the Honorable Dennis J. Curran, retired Massachusetts Superior Court Justice. A judge for 15 years, Curran presided over 450 civil and criminal trials. The author of 42 book chapters and articles, he has taught at Tufts University, Roger Williams University of School of Law, and Brown University.

result.title: Liberty and reformation in the Puritan Revolution
result.creator: Haller, William, 1885-1974
description: xv, 410 pages ; 24 cm

"Treating revolutionary Puritanism as a great dynamic force, this book picks up where the author's famous The Rise of Puritanism left off, and tells the story of the Puritan argument for freedom and reform from the convening of parliament in 1640 to the fall of the monarchy and the disruption of the church in 1649. When Puritan preachers called upon parliament to cast off the authority of bishops and erect a godly preaching ministry throughout the realm, parliament asked the preachers to draft a scheme of reformation by free discussion. Free discussion, however, led to disagreement about the nature and extent of reform intended. Soon both the press and public became involved in the argument. Men of varying interests, such as William Walwyn and John Milton, began raising questions as to the scope and function of liberty within society--of liberty of conscience, of thought and expression, of preaching and the press, of religious and political association, of legal status, of economic enterprise and social opportunity. The effect was to set Puritans at odds among themselves. The discussion was taken up by unorthodox preachers like John Goodwin, by popular agitators and party organizers like Lilburne, and by the Army. The question became one of how, with the church disrupted, to establish and maintain spiritual unity and constitutional order in the community."--Back book cover
Includes bibliographical references (pages 359-385) and index

result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Special Committee on Ways and Means Reviews PPSD FY2027 Budget – May 28, 2026 The Special Committee on Ways and Means, chaired by Miguel Sanchez, met on May 28, 2026, at 5:37 PM. The committee heard a detailed presentation from Providence Public School District (PPSD) leadership on the proposed FY2027 budget, which faces a $1.3 million decline in state aid and uses $3.2 million from reserves. The discussion covered enrollment declines, charter school tuition pressures, staffing reductions, and support for students experiencing homelessness. ### Appointment to Zoning Board - After being moved out of order, the committee approved the appointment of Mr. Scott to a full term on the Zoning Board. Mr. Scott had served as second alternate since 2019 and replaced Chairman Greenfield. The motion passed unanimously on a voice vote. ### Discussion Items - **Budget Overview:** PPSD leadership (Superintendent, Deputy Superintendent, and Chief of Operations) presented the FY2027 budget. Key challenges include declining enrollment (from 23,000 to ~19,000 students), rising fixed costs (transportation, special education tuition, benefits), and a loss of state aid due to fewer students and lower poverty rates. The district has reduced staff by over 500 FTEs since the start of state intervention, including 22 teacher layoffs for the coming year (total of 109 FTE reduction, 4%). - **Revenue:** State aid is projected at $211.3 million, a $1.3 million decline from FY2026. The city contribution is based on a settlement agreement. To balance the budget, the district plans to use $3.2 million from its reserve fund, reducing the reserve from $4.2 million to $1 million. A potential state funding formula change (increasing the success factor from 40% to 43%) could add $4–4.5 million, but the district did not assume that in planning. - **Expenditures:** Transportation costs increased 15% due to a new contract; the district reduced bus runs by four, saving $400,000. Special education tuition rose 8%, though 24 fewer students are placed out-of-district. Custodial contract extension includes a 3.5% annual escalator. The district reduced planned Chromebook purchases (saving $2 million) and eliminated some central office positions, including the grants writer and an MLL manager, through merging roles. - **Staffing and Layoffs:** The 22 teacher layoffs are primarily in areas of declining enrollment (elementary teachers without ESL certification, business education). The district continues to recruit math, special education, and science teachers. As of the meeting, there were fewer than 60 vacancies, down from mid-70s the previous year. Council members expressed concern about messaging around layoffs versus vacancies. - **Charter School Tuition:** Chair Sanchez highlighted that charter school tuition has risen from $21 million in FY2021 to $35.5 million in FY2026, and called this trend “unsustainable.” Several councilors echoed concerns about the fiscal impact of charter expansion on the district, noting that the funding formula does not allow the district to reduce costs proportionally when students leave. The district noted the enrollment loss transition fund softens the blow but is not sufficient. - **Homeless Student Support:** The district serves 133 students experiencing homelessness (7% of enrollment), providing wraparound services, transportation, and supplies. The district is required to transport students even if they temporarily reside outside Providence, costing $1.2 million annually. Academic outcomes for homeless students are significantly lower (e.g., 7% gap in ELA proficiency). Council members asked about data collection and federal grant funding. - **UCAP Program Closure:** The district ended its partnership with UCAP (a middle school program), affecting 42 seventh graders returning to the district. The district created a cohort program at Roger Williams Middle School with additional interventions at a fraction of the previous cost ($1.9 million for UCAP vs. much less for internal services). Only four of the 42 students have IEPs. Councilor Picardo expressed reservations about the transition plan and requested more detailed information. - **Procurement Transition:** Concerns were raised about potential delays in procurement as the district returns to local control. Councilor Davidson’s working group is developing recommendations to maintain efficient procurement while ensuring fiscal oversight. - **Technology and Cybersecurity:** Following a cybersecurity attack last year (no ransom paid), the district implemented new endpoint protection (Falcon) and applied for a grant for employee training. The district also discussed its use of Canvas (LMS) and iReady, noting that iReady is part of a broader Curriculum Associates package and that they monitor the class action lawsuit regarding student data privacy. - **PCTA Facility:** Council members raised concerns about the closure of PCTA for summer recreation programs (impacting 400+ children) due to maintenance; the district expects the facility to be available next summer. Alternative sites (Hope High School) have capacity and cleanliness issues. ### Key Outcomes - The committee voted to **continue items 1–5** (budget items) without a final vote, pending final state revenue numbers and further discussion at the school board. The budget will return for final approval in September. - The appointment to the Zoning Board was **approved unanimously**. - The meeting was **adjourned** after a motion by Councilor Davidson, seconded by Councilor Graves. - The committee plans further meetings to deepen partnership with PPSD as it returns to local control.

result.title: Rhode Island History Digital Collection
result.description: The John Carter Brown Library and the Redwood Library and Athenaeum are Rhode Island institutions with distinct, but complementary, collections. To lay the foundation for a Rhode Island History Digital Collection the two libraries are collaborating on a project to scan the unique documents representing the earliest chapters of the region. The Redwood Library holds some unique manuscript records of early Rhode Island and the John Carter Brown Library holds seminal works by Roger Williams, Rhode Island's founder and innovator, as well as materials relating to religion, native peoples, conflicts with native peoples and the British government, boundary issues, business, daily life, and education. THE REDWOOD LIBRARY AND ATHENAEUM is one of the first lending libraries in America, housed in the oldest lending library building in the country. Founded in 1747 by forty-six proprietors upon the principle of "having nothing in view but the good of mankind," its mission continues over 265 years later. The Library's core collections include the original collection of 1522 volumes gathered by the first proprietors and printed materials related to the history of Newport and Aquidneck Island that far exceed the collecting scope of any other regional cultural institution. THE JOHN CARTER BROWN LIBRARY is an independently administered and funded center for advanced research in history and the humanities, founded in 1846 and located at Brown University since 1901. Housed within the library's walls is an internationally renowned collection of primary historical sources pertaining to North and South America from the time of its discovery by Europeans (ca. 1492) until the end of the colonial period (ca. 1825).

Text of dead reads: Know all men, that I Myantonomy, cheefe sachem of the Nanheygansett have sold unto the persons heare named, one parsell of lands with all the rights and privileges theroff whatsoever lyinge uppon the west syde of that part of the sea called Sowhanes Bay, from Copassanatuxett, over against a little island in the sayd bay, being the north bounds, and the outmost point that neck of land called Shawhomet; beinge the south bounds ffrom the sea shoare of each boundary uppon a straight lyne westward twentie miles: I say I have truely sould this parsell of land above sayde, the proportion whereof is according to the mapp under written or drawne, being the forme of it, onto Randall Houlden, John Greene, John Wickes, Ffrancis Weston, Samuell Gorton, Richard Waterman, John Warner, Richard Carder, Sampson Shotten, Robert Potter, William Wuddall ffor one hundredth and fortie ffathom of wampumpeage, I say I have sould it, and possession of it given unto the men, above sayd, with the ffree and joynt consent of the present inhabitants being natives, as it appeares by their hands hereunto annexed. Dated ye twelfth day of January 1642. Beinge enacted oppon the above sayd parsell of land un the presence off sachem of Shawhomett. Pum homm Myantonomy [with his bow and arrow seal] Jano [bird] his marke Totanomans his mark [gun?] John Greene, junr

Deed of Warwick is on p. [1], followed by hand drawn map, with commentary, of the area sold on p. [2], followed by practice of the beginning sentence of the deed on p. [3], which is backed with thicker paper and is blank on p. [4]

Canonicus, uncle of chief sachem Miantonomo, deeded to Roger Williams land that would become Providence Plantations; here Miantonomo, sells the land that would become Warwick to Samuel Gorton and others
John Carter Brown Library copy is housed within a brown leather folder, measuring 31 cm. in height, with cover title: Deed of Warwick, R.I: from the Indians, 1642

John Carter Brown Library copy has the larger transcription of the deed, along with a smaller transcription of the deed in the hand of John Russell Bartlett, and a letter addressed to John Nicholas Brown, dated 1885, with information on the repair of the deed housed in JCB bibliographical file
