result.description: Profiles in History: Autograph Catalog 48 2009 Histoical48 (Highlights of the entire catalog) Chronological Timeline of Major Historical Letters & Documents: This timeline tracks the most significant handwritten letters, military directives, and diplomatic dispatches from the catalog, ordered by the date they were written. 1776 – John Hancock Directive: President of Continental Congress demands winter troops. 1778 – George Washington Military Orders: Pursues retreating British to Battle of Monmouth. 1780 – Thomas Jefferson Governor Letter: Defends Virginia coast from British fleet. 1780 -John Adams Guardianship Note: Hands care of grandson to Franklin. 1781 – Benjamin Franklin Passy Letter: Laments lost papers to a traitor. 1784 – Daniel Boone Land Survey: Drafted for his young orphaned nephew. 1784 – George Washington 17-Page Letter: Settles legal battle during active warfare. 1786 – John Adams Minister Dispatch: Bemoans hostile post-war relations with Britain. 1792 – Thomas Jefferson Congressional Acts: Lists acts bailing out Greene's estate. 1801 – James Monroe Diplomatic Introduction: Pre-negotiation track for Louisiana Purchase. 1804 – James Monroe Minister Letter: Outlines global anxieties over Emperor Napoleon. 1805 – James Madison Wine Logistics: Shipping Lisbon wine for capital parties. 1810 – James Madison Garden Request: Hires future first White House gardener. 1815 – James Monroe War Dispatch: Organizes ship unknowingly delivering peace treaty. 1822 – Andrew Jackson Power of Attorney: Establishes formal founding of Memphis, Tennessee. 1832 – John Quincy Adams Masonic Critique: Denounces secret blood oaths after murder. 1857 – Abraham Lincoln Legal Advice: Attorney letter prior to "House Divided". 1861 – Abraham Lincoln Executive Letter: Pairs with an anti-slavery editor. 1865 – William T. Sherman Manifesto: Outlines total war field command directives. 1892 – Mark Twain Immigration Defense: Supports preserving native languages at home. 1919 – John Reed Bolshevik Defense: Eyewitness report favoring Russian Revolution. 1919–1920 – Wilson & Taft Archive: 19-letter clash over Treaty of Versailles. 1927 – Marie Curie Vellum Quotation: Invokes Pasteur declaring science beats war. 1929 – Arthur Conan Doyle Statement: Believes WWI victors suffered like vanquished. 1932 – H.G. Wells Pax Mundi Essay: Demands world federation to secure peace. 1956 – Harry S. Truman Travel Critique: Witty art critique of uncircumcised David. 1967 – J.D. Salinger Reclusive Letter: Candidly reveals love for Islamic mysticism. Another highlight of the catalog is The Civile War Archive.  It includes documents defining the battlefield, ideologies, and aftermath of the conflict. Tactical Commands & Scorched Earth Doctrine William T. Sherman's "Total War" Manifesto (1865): Four-page field letter written in pencil to Gen. Gillmore commanding absolute infrastructural destruction of Southern rails and boilers to force mass desertions in Lee's army. David Dixon Porter Fleet Letter (1865): Civil War naval correspondence defending a commander's tactical line movement under heavy blast fire during the assaults on Fort Fisher. Abraham Lincoln's Administration & Legal Foundations Springfield Legal Brief (c. 1853): Early document completely handwritten and signed under his prominent law firm partnership "Lincoln & Herndon". Executive Introduction Letter (1861): Penned two months into his presidency to introduce Treasury Secretary Salmon P. Chase to an outspoken anti-slavery Republican newspaperman. Wartime Application Endorsement (1863): Autograph endorsement signed as President routing a soldier's application for Assistant Paymaster to Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton. Presidential Appointments Collection: Civil War executive documents appointing Marshals and Consuls to international territories like Munich, Argentina, and Russia, all countersigned by Secretary of State William H. Seward. Abolitionist Ideology & Battle Anthems Robert Gould Shaw Pre-Command Letter (1862): Deeply revealing 8-page letter home to his sister criticizing demoralized Union command and defending his views on Emancipation five months before leading the historic all-Black 54th Massachusetts Volunteers. George Frederick Root Martial Anthem (1881): Signed autograph musical quotation featuring the handwritten opening bars and lyrics to the defining Union rally song "The Battle Cry of Freedom". William T. Sherman Portrait (1870): Formal portrait signed by Sherman during his post-war leadership as Commander of the Army. The catalog ends with the Woodrow Wilson & William H. Taft Historic Archive (Treaty of Versailles), this 19-letter collection includes 2 presidential letters from Wilson and 17 letters from former President Taft, all sent to Edward E. Whiting, Editor of The Boston Evening Record. Woodrow Wilson’s Correspondence Letter #1 (November 19, 1920): Corrects an editorial claiming he refused to sign a ratified treaty (p. 22). Clarifies that the Senate never sent him a treaty with reservations, but simply notified him that ratification failed (p. 22). Letter #2 (December 1, 1920): Thanks the editor for his sense of honor in publicly correcting the newspaper's error (p. 22). William Howard Taft’s Correspondence (Key Excerpts) May 5, 1919: Warns that a Republican blockade of the treaty would be a "suicidal policy" for the party. May 20, 1919: Attacks Senate Majority Leader Henry Cabot Lodge’s stance, predicting Lodge is "reckoning without his fist". June 4, 1919: Slams machine Republicans who oppose the League of Nations simply because they "hate Wilson". July 15, 1919: Expresses fear that Irish-Americans protesting the League will trigger a backlash against "hyphenated Americanism". September 12, 1919: Faults Wilson's rigid "schoolmaster" speaking style for using contemptuous phrases that alienated swing-vote Senators. December 15, 1919: Labels Wilson a "mountain of Egotism" and a fool for refusing to compromise after the treaty's initial defeat. March 25, 1920: Blames Wilson as the primary cause for the treaty's final defeat, noting Wilson had the power to save it but declined. November 12, 1920: Pins his final expectations for American internationalism on a new administration with a handwritten note: "Our sole hope is in Harding". November 27, 1920: Argues against Lodge's claim that Harding's landslide election victory was a public referendum against the League. Comprehensive Summary of All Signatures in the catalog: Historical Figures, Founding Fathers, US Presidents, Statesmen, First Ladies Theodore Roosevelt (Lot Cover Image): A signed and inscribed photograph dated November 21, 1804. John Adams (Lot 1): An ALS from 1780 arranging for Benjamin Franklin to take over the guardianship of young Samuel Cooper Johonnot in Paris while Adams traveled to Amsterdam. John Adams (Lot 2): An ALS from 1786 written from London expressing deep remorse and pessimism regarding the broken, hostile state of relations between the US and Great Britain right after the War of Independence. John Quincy Adams (Lot 3): A monumental 1808 letter defending his highly controversial support of President Thomas Jefferson's Embargo Act, a political stance that cost Adams his Senate seat just two months later. John Quincy Adams (Lot 4): A superb 1832 letter fiercely criticizing the Freemasons for their graphic and barbarous blood oaths following the infamous 1826 kidnapping and murder of masonic critic William Morgan. Andrew Jackson (Lot 6): An exceptionally historic 1822 manuscript document officially establishing the power of attorney and land ratifications that marked the formal genesis and founding layout of Memphis, Tennessee. Daniel Boone (Lot 14): An exceedingly rare 1784 hand-drawn land survey and document drafted for his 16-year-old nephew, Joseph, whose father had been killed by Native Americans while hunting with Daniel four years prior. Marie Curie (Lot 19): A 1927 vellum quotation written in French invoking Louis Pasteur to declare that science and peace will ultimately triumph over ignorance and war. Dwight D. Eisenhower (Lot 28): A touching, wartime love letter written to his wife Mamie from the African front in 1943, telling her not to worry about press rumors of his capture. Millard Fillmore (Lot 32): A rare, boldly signed and dated full-length Carte de Visite photograph from 1866. Benjamin Franklin (Lot 33): A remarkable 1781 letter written from France to his son-in-law reflecting on how political might can subdue moral right, lamenting historical papers lost to a traitorous friend, and giving educational advice for his grandson. Warren G. Harding (Lot 39): A personal, 4-page handwritten letter from Christmas Day, 1904 . Writing to the father of his future White House Secretary, the 39-year-old Harding shares a humorous holiday message about trying to buy a "new set of nerves" from Santa Claus. John Hancock (Lot 40): An urgent 1776 military directive signed as President of the Continental Congress. Penned just four months after signing the Declaration of Independence and following a costly defeat at Long Island, Hancock desperately implores the states to supply troops and ammunition before winter. Herbert Hoover (Lot 45): A formal inscribed and signed waist-up portrait photograph of the elder statesman. Thomas Jefferson (Lot 47): A 1792 manuscript circular letter signed as Secretary of State. Jefferson enumerates 21 historic acts passed during the first session of the Second Congress, notably highlighting the federal act to indemnify the heavily indebted estate of Revolutionary War hero General Nathanael Greene. Thomas Jefferson (Lot 48): An intimate 1820 handwritten letter sent from Monticello to his presidential protégé, James Monroe. Jefferson forwards an application on behalf of an aging revolutionary veteran, demonstrating the enduring personal bond and political alliance between the two Virginia Founders. Thomas Jefferson (Lot 49): A critical 1780 wartime military letter signed as Governor of Virginia. Facing a looming British naval threat in the Chesapeake Bay, Jefferson orders a countermand to delay militia reinforcement movements to protect local soil. Thomas Jefferson (Lot 50): An 1805 signed presidential endorsement approving George Day as the Keeper of the Squam Lighthouse in Massachusetts—a post Day would faithfully hold for the next 45 years. Lyndon B. Johnson (Lot 51): A 1964 presidential typed letter on White House stationery thanking a friend for a handsomely engraved money clip that was uniquely designed with a John F. Kennedy half-dollar. John F. Kennedy (Lot 52): A charming, handwritten note penned as a U.S. Senator on a vintage United Airlines DC-7 postcard to a fellow flight passenger. Robert F. Kennedy (Lot 53): A handsome inscribed and signed black-and-white portrait photograph of the prominent U.S. Attorney General. Abraham Lincoln (Lot 56): An 1863 presidential handwritten endorsement passed along to his Secretary of War, Edwin M. Stanton, backing a military candidate for an Assistant Paymastership based on his upright habits in battle. Abraham Lincoln (Lot 57): An 1857 legal letter written as a Springfield attorney giving advice on securing governmental land patents. It represents a pivotal career moment, drafted just one year before his famous "House Divided" speech. Abraham Lincoln (Lot 58): A brief 1861 handwritten letter from the Executive Mansion written exactly two months into his presidency. Lincoln introduces his Secretary of the Treasury, Salmon P. Chase, to an outspoken, anti-slavery Republican newspaperman. Abraham Lincoln (Lot 59): An early, rare legal brief handwritten around 1853 and signed under his successful Springfield law firm partnership name, "Lincoln & Herndon". Abraham Lincoln (Lots 60, 61, 62, 63, & 64): A collection of five highly valuable civil and military documents signed as President. These include official appointments of regional Marshals, international Consuls for the Argentine Republic, Munich, and Russia, as well as an 1863 Naval appointment for a Lieutenant Commander who fought at Fort Fisher. James Madison (Lot 68): An 1810 handwritten letter sent as President to James Monroe. Madison requests the temporary services of a highly regarded gardener named Charles Bizet to cultivate the grounds at Montpelier; Bizet would later make history as the very first official gardener of the White House. James Madison (Lot 69): A 1805 handwritten letter as Secretary of State coordinating a secure shipment of imported Lisbon wine from Baltimore to Washington during a burgeoning "golden social era" in the capital. James Monroe (Lot 72): An 1804 handwritten letter sent while serving as Minister to Great Britain. Writing home to Virginia immediately after Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor, Monroe breaks down European political anxieties and America's firm stance on maintaining neutrality. James Monroe (Lot 73): An exceptional 1801 letter to James Madison serving as an introduction to French Consul Cambacérès. This historic document captures the direct personal and diplomatic genesis that paved the way for the legendary Louisiana Purchase negotiations. James Monroe (Lot 74): A monumentally historic 1815 State Department letter organizing a dispatch vessel to Europe. Unbeknownst to Monroe at the time due to slow communication, the Treaty of Ghent had already been signed weeks prior to end the War of 1812; that exact vessel would return carrying the physical peace treaty to President Madison. Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax (Lot 75): A 1715 treasury document authorizing a dividend payout for South Sea Stock. It represents an artifact from the earliest stages of the historic "South Sea Bubble," an early experiment in public stock ownership that led to a catastrophic global financial crash in 1720. James K. Polk & James Buchanan (Lot 79): An 1845 presidential appointment document signed by Polk and countersigned by Buchanan as Secretary of State. Ronald Reagan (Lot 84): A handsome signed publicity photograph from his early Hollywood acting days. Ronald Reagan (Lot 85): An Autograph Letter Signed ("Ron") on crested stationery sharing a humorous, real-life Irish tombstone joke he discovered while researching his family genealogy in Ireland. Eleanor Roosevelt (Lot 90): An elegant 1941 portrait photograph signed as First Lady, showing her seated at her White House desk next to a framed photo of FDR. Franklin D. Roosevelt (Lot 91): A signed sepia portrait photograph inscribed to a Democratic congressman from New York. Theodore Roosevelt (Lot 92): A superb 1907 oversized photograph signed as President, affectionately inscribed to his personal family physician. Theodore Roosevelt (Lot 93): An incredible 1904 oversized portrait signed as President, capturing him in full uniform outside his military tent during his legendary "Rough Rider" Spanish-American War days. Harry S. Truman (Lot 104): A fascinating, 4-page handwritten letter from 1956 to Dean Acheson recapping his first European tour. It contains incredibly candid observations, including meeting Winston Churchill and a witty art critique noting that Michelangelo's famous statue of David was not circumcised. George Washington (Lot 109): A magnificent, massive 17-page handwritten letter from 1784 to Signer of the Declaration Francis Lightfoot Lee. Washington details his immense personal frustration trying to settle a 10-year legal battle and family feud over an old friend's estate while simultaneously serving on the battlefield as Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army. George Washington (Lot 110): A major 1778 Revolutionary War letter signed as Commander-in-Chief to Brig. Gen. Woodford. Written at 4:00 AM immediately following the British evacuation of Philadelphia, Washington orders immediate troop movements to pursue the enemy across New Jersey, culminating in the Battle of Monmouth. Woodrow Wilson & William H. Taft (Lot 117): A highly historic political archive consisting of 2 letters signed by President Wilson and 17 letters signed by former President Taft. Written to a Boston newspaper editor, the correspondence provides a raw look at their bitter clash over the Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations. Historical Figures, Music, Artists, Masters, Aviation, Dance, Hollywood & Entertainment Pier Angeli (Lot 7): A signed and inscribed vintage publicity photograph from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. Fred Astaire & Janis Paige (Lot 8): A color MGM publicity still for the 1957 musical film Silk Stockings, signed by both actors. Lauren Bacall (Lot 9): A signed black-and-white publicity photograph of the actress posing in a stylish jumpsuit. Ray Bolger (Lot 10): A signed and inscribed vintage sepia portrait of the famous stage and film actor. The Beatles (Lot 11): An incredibly rare early promotional photograph depicting original drummer Pete Best, but signed on the reverse by all four band members—including his eventual replacement, Ringo Starr. Humphrey Bogart & Lauren Bacall (Lot 13): A dual-signed color publicity photograph from their classic film Key Largo. Frank Capra (Lot 15): A signed and inscribed pensive headshot portrait of the legendary film director in his later years. Lon Chaney Sr. (Lot 16): A rare signed portrait of the silent film star in character as the gangster leader "Chuck Collins" from MGM's The Big City. William F. "Buffalo Bill" Cody (Lot 17): An extraordinary autograph statement where Cody handwrites the answers to two prompt questions, explaining exactly how he earned his nickname (killing 4,280 buffalo for railroad workers) and detailing the battle where he killed Cheyenne Chief Yellow Hand. Chuck Connors (Lot 18): A signed publicity photograph of the actor in character as Lucas McCain from the hit western series The Rifleman. Marlene Dietrich (Lot 21): A 1941 Universal Pictures legal contract signed by the actress to extend her employment services for the classic western film The Spoilers. Miles Davis (Lot 20): A rare signed black-and-white postcard photograph depicting the iconic jazz pioneer holding his trumpet. Marlene Dietrich (Lot 22): An oversized, vintage matte-finish portrait photograph inscribed by the actress. Walt Disney (Lot 23): A rare, oversized sepia portrait photograph from early in his career, boldly inscribed and signed by Disney. Sergei Eisenstein (Lot 29): A rare 1943 letter written in red pencil on official studio letterhead by the "Father of the Montage" during the production of his historical epic film Ivan the Terrible. Federico Fellini (Lot 30): A signed and inscribed photograph of the revered Italian director captured on a movie set in Rome. John Ford (Lot 31): A vintage 1928 print signed by director John Ford alongside seven principal cast members of his silent drama film Four Sons. George Gershwin (Lot 34): A signed and inscribed light sepia photograph from 1929 showing the legendary composer seated at his piano. George Gershwin (Lot 35): A magnificent 1926 typed letter featuring an authentic, hand-penned autograph musical quotation of his iconic masterpiece, "Rhapsody in Blue". Jack Haley & Margaret Hamilton (Lots 37 & 38): Individual, inscribed publicity photographs signed in character from The Wizard of Oz. Haley signs as the "Tin Man" alongside Dorothy and the crew, while Hamilton pens a wonderfully witty, damp-themed inscription as the "Wicked Witch of the West" right as her character melts. Rita Hayworth (Lot 41): A gorgeous inscribed photograph signed in character as the ultimate femme fatale from her iconic, culturally defining 1946 role in Gilda. Audrey Hepburn (Lot 42): A 1962 Universal City legal contract signed by the actress and humanitarian, modifying her film production terms and post-photography looping schedule for the Paris-based classic Charade. Charlton Heston (Lot 43): A signed movie publicity still depicting the actor in character as Michelangelo painting the Sistine Chapel from The Agony and the Ecstasy. Buddy Holly & The Crickets (Lot 44): An incredibly rare, full-band page signed in blue ink by all four rock 'n' roll musicians from "The Biggest Show of Stars For ’57" program, featuring Holly's exceptionally scarce autograph. Vivien Leigh & Laurence Olivier (Lots 54 & 55): Exceptional Hollywood collectibles, including a romantic dual-signed portrait of the renowned acting couple, alongside a beautiful individual portrait of Leigh signed in character as her pivotal, career-defining role as Scarlett O’Hara in Gone With the Wind. Charles A. Lindbergh (Lots 65 & 66): Commemorative aviation pieces signed by "The Lone Eagle". It features a signed 1928 custom lithograph celebrating his historic 1927 non-stop transatlantic flight to Paris, alongside an airfield postcard next to The Spirit of St. Louis. Ernst Lubitsch (Lot 67): A 1932 typed letter written in German on Hotel Adlon stationery by the prominent German-born Jewish film comedy director. Glenn Miller (Lot 71): An inscribed and signed photograph of the legendary American Jazz bandleader pictured holding his trombone. Waslaw Nijinsky (Lot 76): A superb, formal 1913 cabinet photograph signed by the world-famous Russian ballet virtuoso. Rembrandt Peale (Lot 77): An extraordinary 3-page 1808 letter written to his wife from Paris describing his travels through Europe to study the brushwork of masters like Rubens, Raphael, and Titian to blend their systems into his own art. "Our Gang" Cast (Lot 78): An incredibly rare, oversized vintage photograph signed by six of the original juvenile cast members (including Farina, Harry Spear, and Joe Cobb) alongside Pete the Pup. Ferdinand Anton Ernst "Ferry" Porsche (Lot 81): A signed portrait photograph of the legendary Austrian sports car designer and automotive pioneer. Cole Porter (Lot 82): A wonderful signed autograph musical quotation from 1961 featuring a hand-penned bar of music from his hit song "In the Still of the Night". George Reeves (Lot 87): A rare signed portrait of the actor best known for his definitive 1950s television portrayal of Superman. Frederic Remington (Lot 88): A handwritten letter from his New Rochelle home connecting an art buyer with a friend seeking to purchase Remington's signature Western masterpiece, "Bucking Broncho". John D. Rockefeller (Lot 89): A rare photograph signed by the aged industrial titan and Standard Oil founder at his desk in Florida. George Frederick Root (Lot 94): An 1881 autograph musical quotation featuring the opening bars and lyrics to his iconic Civil War martial anthem, "The Battle Cry of Freedom". Jonas E. Salk (Lot 96): A signed color photograph of the virologist holding a medical syringe next to two children, celebrating his historic development of the polio vaccine. Thomas Sully (Lot 100): An 1839 letter by the prominent portrait painter discussing the shipment of his portrait of Colonel John J. Abert, a historic artwork that now hangs at West Point. Piotr Illich Tchaikovsky (Lot 102): An exceptional 1887 portrait cabinet photograph signed and inscribed in Cyrillic by the legendary Russian Romantic composer. Mark Twain (Lot 105): A beautiful 1892 handwritten letter written from Lake Como, Italy, passionately defending the right of immigrants in America to preserve and speak their native languages at home. Mark Twain (Lots 106, 107, & 108): A stellar group of three distinct signed autograph aphorisms featuring some of his most famous, witty adages: "When in doubt, tell the truth", "Be good & you will be lonesome", and "It is better to deserve honors & not have them, than have them & not deserve them". Jack Webb (Lot 111): A signed publicity photograph of the prominent actor and television producer. Billy Wilder (Lot 112): A 1937 Paramount Pictures certificate of authorship signed by the filmmaker certifying his screenwriting collaboration on the comedy Bluebeard's 8th Wife. Billy Wilder (Lot 113): A signed publicity photograph showing the iconic director guiding Jack Lemmon on the movie set of The Front Page. Fay Wray (Lot 114): A spectacular vintage photograph signed by the actress, showing her trapped in the massive prop shackles used to hold the beast in the original 1933 blockbuster King Kong. H.G. Wells (Lot 115): A profound autograph statement (c. 1925–1932) by the famous science fiction author arguing that sentimentalizing peace is foolish and that true world peace can only be achieved through a unified world federation. Andrew Wyeth (Lot 116): A rare vintage photograph signed and inscribed by the prominent mid-20th-century American painter. Military Heroes, War Diaries, Historical Movements Frederick W. Habel (Lot 36): A riveting, highly detailed 10-page handwritten battle diary. As a crew member aboard the USS Nevada, Habel captures a raw, first-hand account of the D-Day Invasion of Normandy, documenting minefields, downed planes, and using the ship's 14-inch guns against German troop movements. Jacklyn Lucas, George Wahlen, & Charles W. Lindberg (Lot 46): A stirring, dual-Medal of Honor and Silver Star signed photograph. All three distinct WWII heroes autographed a dramatic photograph capturing the historic first flag-raising atop Mt. Suribachi during the brutal battle of Iwo Jima. Anthony C. McAuliffe (Lot 70): A bold signature card accompanied by a photograph of the U.S. Army General. It includes his legendary wartime sentiment and single-word defiance to a German surrender ultimatum during the Battle of the Bulge: "Nuts!". David Dixon Porter (Lot 83): A Civil War-date letter signed in 1865 by the U.S. Naval Admiral defending a ship commander's actions during the intense Union naval assaults on Fort Fisher. John Silas "Jack" Reed (Lot 86): A rare 1919 letter written by the radical American journalist and activist fiercely defending the Bolsheviks and Marxian policies after witnessing the Russian Revolution firsthand. William T. Sherman (Lot 95): An impressive 1870 Mathew Brady cabinet photograph signed by the Union General during his tenure as Commander of the Army. William T. Sherman (Lot 97): A monumentally historic Civil War letter written in pencil from the field in 1865. Sherman commands General Gillmore to target Confederate infrastructure, perfectly personifying his controversial concept of "total war" and the psychological destruction of civilian resources to break the South. Robert Gould Shaw (Lot 98): A rare 8-page Civil War letter written in 1862 to his sister. Shaw laments the poor state of the Union command and defends his views on Emancipation five months before taking command of the famous, all-Black 54th Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry.

result.description: "Oops, Shorts in the Winter" Horse Racing Names Poem by Joe A Pasquale, Dec 18th 2024 Tampa Bay Downs. Joseph A Pasquale's poetry collection was recently added to the national archive in the National Horse Racing Hall of Fame in Saratoga Springs, New York. All horse racing haiku poems are constructed only using Horse Racing  Names and are 100% human generated, no AI use. All used words are from USA Horse Racing Names, all horses ran same day on USA horse racing tracks from Races on Dec 15th 2024. All Photography, Art, and Haiku by Joseph A Pasquale. Joseph A Pasquale is an American author who writes in a variety of literary genres, including poetry, memoir, and literary fiction. Pasquale's poetry collection, "Kindred Spirits: Horse Racing Name Poems" was published by Adelaide Books in 2020. https://www.amazon.com/Kindre.../dp/B08KTGZDBK/ref=sr_1_1 ... Joe A Pasquale is also known as The Horse Racing Poet and also writes in London, Ireland and the UK. www.HorseRacingPoet.com www.josephapasquale.com Horse Racing Name Haiku Poem Prayer Production Date: 12-15-2024. From Races on Dec 15th 2024 all over the USA. Follow more on: Instagram and Twitter https://www.instagram.com/horseracingpoet/ https://x.com/HorseRacingPoet Joseph A Pasquale is an American author who writes in a variety of literary genres, including poetry, memoir, and literary fiction. He has written over 65 books of prose, including poetry. He was born in Worcester, MA and studied the art of writing literary fiction under bestselling-author, Ken Eulo. Ken Eulo served as his editor on two finished suspense novels. Joseph A Pasquale is also a literary writer. In March 2024, Pasquale finished writing, editing and revising a new novel, "Upon them, A Childhood Cast,” also known as “Shrewsbury Street.” The novel is over 800 - 1000 pages. There are accompanying writings outside of the book spanning about 500+ pages (untyped in handwriting). This novel either completes, or nearly completes Pasquale's body of prose novel literary works. Joseph A Pasquale's poetry collection was recently added to the national archive in the National Horse Racing Hall of Fame in Saratoga Springs, New York.  Pasquale was published in the Hollywood hardback, "Literary (and other) Celebrity Doodles" Volume II. (published 2019) Pasquale and Margaret C Arana were both interviewed and have a spotlight in the Hollywood hardback, "The Musso & Frank Grill" (published 2019). Pasquale was a regular at Mussos. Pasquale's poetry collection, "Kindred Spirits: Horse Racing Name Poems" was published by Adelaide Books in 2020. Joe A Pasquale is also known as The Horse Racing Poet and he writes in London, IRELAND, UK and USA.  www.HorseRacingPoet.com He is the nephew to Andrea Tempesta who penned the Worcester novel, “Afloat A Stranger’s Shore.” His father was friends with Larry J Sandners who penned the Worcester novel, "Children Sad: Blackhawks," which Joseph A Pasquale rescued from being lost in 2024.  Joe A Pasquale is the author of The LOVE JUNKY series spanning over 3000 pages (unpublished). Over 8 novels in the series including his unpublished 700 page LA novel. Pasquale is the creator of Daily Terrors TV and Peter S Fogg, a pen name he writes under and has published books (under the pen name). Pasquale created the Confession Booth Terrors and Blood Diaries and Confessions of Preacher Aaron stories.  Joseph A Pasquale's horse racing poetry collection was recently added to the national archive in the National Horse Racing Hall of Fame in Saratoga Springs, New York. His photography, art and books are for sale by contact at his website: www.josephapasquale.com

But the many sources here generally ques- tion the Administration's logic. They say the dissidents appear to have closed ranks with the Colonel, at least temporarily, in a show of nationalism against a foreign threat. One diplomat with particularly close ties toy the military reported that many of those in, the military who are doubters of Qaddafi are; in fact elated over the outcome of the fight- ing. Despite having suffered a pubicly unde-1 termined number of casualties and damage to boats, planes and a radar site, they see Libya - and themselves - as a David that has stood up against the American Goliath. 'Misreading' Is Seen "The Americans are misreading the inter- nal situation," said one diplomat. Some of the diplomats acknowledge that in the murkiness of Libyan politics, American military pressure could prove to be effective in the long term. But the consensus among the many sources is that the best policy to get rid of Colonel Qaddafi is to leave him to his own designs. They say his erratic political behavior and his failing economic policies in the face of plummeting oil prices are fanning dissension on their own. Libyans are being inconvenienced by shortages in food and consumer products, while many of the colonel's grandiose con- struction projects have becomed mired in mismanagement and debt. Falling income from oil has meant that the country can no longer buy its way out of its problems. "Qaddafi is his worst enemy," said one dip- lomat. Secretiveness in Libya, which is saturated by a pervasive intelligence network, makes the extent of the dissent inside the military difficult to measure. But at least seven assas- sination attempts, most of them by military men, have been reported in recent years. Efforts to Displace Military TRIPOLI, Libya 1#-,~ April 3 - When Col. And, traveling or not, he wears a bulletproof vest, even under'casual clothes at home, according to those who have been around him. These measures are part of the extraordi- nary security that surrounds the man, whose homeitself is a military barracks where tank guns point through slots at passers-by. The security is directed against Colonel Qaddafi's own military. Having taken power himself in a military coup 16 years -ago, the colonel is said by. Western and Arab diplo- mats and other observers here to be virtually paranoid about new discontent in the ranks. The Colonel continues making roughly $1 billion a year worth of purchases of Soviet arms, but some 1,400 tanks and 450 combat planes have remained stored, often crated, according to the London-based Inter- national Institute for Strategic Studies. Read in English by LibriVox volunteers Having accidentally placed himself in a compromising situation, Christopher Jedbury, Jr. is forced to marry a woman without ever seeing her. When his father finds out about the marriage he turns Christopher out and sends him to India to work as a lowly clerk in his trading company offices there. The matter of Christopher’s wife becomes complicated when he meets the lovely Dora and asks his lawyer friend to find the mystery bride in order to dissolve the marriage. The plot takes a turn when the wife cannot be found anywhere and Dora reveals she has a secret of her own! WASHINGTON, June 18--A Federal district judge entered a plea of not guilty for Edwin P. Wilson today when the former American intelligence agent declined to plead guilty or not guilty on charges of illegally aiding Libyan ter. rorists. Judge John R. Pratt entered the plea after rejecting a request by Mr. Wil- son's attorney, John A. Keats, that the arraignment here be postponed for a week to give him time to examine the circumstances of Mr. Wilson's capture earlier this week. Mr. Keats said that the Government might have improperly ,apprehended Mr. Wilson and that his client did not want to plead until It had been deter- mined whether he was subject to the jurisdiction of the court. Mr. Wilson was arrested in New York on Tuesday after arriving from the Do- minican Republic. He had traveled there from Libya, apparently in the false belief that he would be given a safe haven. The Dominican authorities, alerted by the American authorities to Mr. Wilson's travel plans, placed him on a nonstop flight to New York after determining that he was traveling under an assumed name on a false Irish passport. Lured Into Trap Justice Department officials have re- fused to provide details about the inter- national trap they set for Mr. Wilson, but some officials have said that he was lured to the Dominican Republic by as- sociates who were secretly cooperating with the department. After refusing to delay the hearing, Judge Pratt called Mr. Wilson before the bench and instructed him to enter a plea on charges including the illegal shipment of explosives to Libya, con- spiracy to commit murder and the ille ' 3 gal export of military g articles. Mr. Wilson declined to enter a plea. Judge Pratt then entered a plea of not'' guilty on his behalf. 11" cr The judge also ordered bail continu at $20 million and gave Mr. Keats a,... month in which to file motions beforvt.',;, the next court proceeding, which is,,. scheduled for July 14. Today's hearing,,., lasted less than 10 minutes. Mr. Wilson and Frank E. Terpil, aA- I other former American intelligence agent, were first indicted in April 1980 on charges stemming from their associ- ation with Libya. The indictment watt' b superseded by a new one last August. According to the Justice Department, hti Mr. Wilson and Mr. Terpil signed a deal:`) in 1976 with Col. Muammar el-Qaddaf?, the leader of Libya, to sell their exper-. tire in intelligence and military matters to Libya and to aid in the establishment of a terrorist training program. The Central Intelligence Agency; which employed both men until the;. early 1970's, has repeatedly denied that it knew about or authorized the Libyan operation. result.description: STS-94 Mission Commander James D. Halsell, Jr., puts his left glove on while he is assisted into his launch/entry suit in the Operations and Checkout (O&C) Building. Halsell is on his fourth space flight, having served as commander of STS-83 and pilot of both STS-74 and STS-65. He is a lieutenant colonel in the Air Force and a former SR-71 Blackbird test pilot and holds master?s degrees in management and space operations. Halsell will have responsibility for the success of the mission and will operate and maintain Columbia during the Red, or second shift. He will also assist with a materials science experiment and a protein crystal growth payload during the 16-day mission. Halsell and six fellow crew members will shortly depart the O&C and head for Launch Pad 39A, where the Space Shuttle Columbia will lift off during a launch window that opens at 1:50 p.m. EDT, July 1. The launch window was opened 47 minutes early to improve the opportunity to lift off before Florida summer rain showers reached the space center

result.title: Sarasota City Commission Regular Meeting – January 5, 2026
result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Sarasota City Commission Regular Meeting – January 5, 2026 The Sarasota City Commission met on January 5, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 3:42 p.m. to address a wide-ranging agenda including board reports, consent items, housing authority collaboration, and the city manager search. The meeting included public comment on noise ordinance enforcement, approval of numerous routine contracts and grants, new board appointments, and a contentious discussion on public parking at McCown Towers. ### Citizens' Input (Noise Ordinance) - **Ronnique Hawkins**, City resident, presented in support of the noise ordinance, displaying an obituary of former Mayor Rev. Dr. Jerome Dupree and videos of late-night disturbances in Newtown. She questioned whether the city is prepared to cover medical bills from noise-related health impacts and asked the Commission to direct the Sarasota Police Department to enforce the ordinance equally citywide and to adopt a 65-decibel limit similar to Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. - **Victor Woods**, a national speaker and Lakewood Ranch resident, spoke in support of noise ordinance enforcement, arguing that the issue disproportionately affects poor and Black residents and is a basic law enforcement matter. He urged the Commission to treat the Newtown noise problem with the same urgency as in affluent neighborhoods. - **Howard Butts** (through Ms. Hawkins) described his own health struggles and sleep deprivation caused by persistent loud music in Newtown. - **A speaker** (likely Frank Martinucci) read a statement concerning revision of the noise ordinance, recommending residential noise zones outside downtown and elimination of the exemption for Sarasota schools. He noted that over 100 residents have signed a petition requesting reduced stadium PA volume and redirected speakers, and expressed concerns about future school construction adding more noise. ### Consent Calendar - **Consent Agenda No. 1** (Items VI.1–VI.8, VI.10, VI.11): Approved unanimously (5-0). These items included: approval for a public art mural at Robert L. Taylor Community Center (VI.1), seventh amendment to lease with Sarasota Sailing Squadron (VI.2), sale of city-owned property at 710 John Ringling Causeway (VI.3), software license extension with Mitchell Humphrey & Co. (VI.4), collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Local No. 173 (VI.5), traffic signal upgrade consulting with Kimley-Horn (VI.6), as-needed architectural services with multiple firms (VI.7), coastal engineering consulting with Cummins Cederberg and Taylor Engineering (VI.8), a piggyback agreement for utility materials (VI.10), and an extension for sodium bisulfite supply (VI.11). - **Consent Agenda No. 2** (Items VII.1–VII.4): Approved unanimously (5-0). Included Resolution 26R-3370 (FDOT public transportation grant along SR 789), Resolution 26R-3371 (budget amendment for Teamster salary increases), Ordinance 25-5572 (amending Downtown Improvement District powers), and Ordinance 26-5587 (revising Affordable Housing Advisory Committee composition). - **Item VI.9** (Network as a Service project with Ferguson Waterworks, $2,215,712.28) was pulled from Consent Agenda No. 1 by Commissioner Ahearn-Koch for discussion. After a brief presentation by Utilities Director Verne Hall and Ferguson representative Tyler Stargel, the item was approved unanimously (5-0). The system will allow remote meter reading and leak detection. ### Board Actions & Reports - **Downtown Improvement District (DID) Annual Report** (Item V.1): Presented by Ronnie Shugar (Chair) and Julie Ryan. Key points: DID supports programs like Fresh Fridays (attracts 2,000–3,000 attendees), Bay Runner Trolley ($50,000 annual support), holiday lighting, and sidewalk maintenance. Commissioners asked about data on economic impact and expansion of district boundaries. The report was accepted unanimously (5-0). - **Employee Retirement Account Committee (ERAC) Annual Report** (Item V.2): Presented by Ben Billingsley (Chair). The DC plan is closed to new participants; 170 active members, 500 total participants. No cost to the city for Corebridge services. Report accepted unanimously (5-0). - **CRA Minutes** (Item CRA.1): Approved unanimously (5-0). - **Newtown CRA Advisory Board Report on RL Taylor Public Art Mural** (Item CRA.2): Presented by Wayne Appleby and Rochelle Gallant. The mural would celebrate Newtown history on the west wall of the community center. The board requested permission to proceed with the public art process. The report was accepted unanimously (5-0), and the consent item (VI.1) was approved as part of Consent Agenda No. 1. ### Board Appointments - **Affordable Housing Advisory Committee (AHAC)** (Item VIII.1): Five applicants were considered for four positions. Cindy Emshoff (OHCD) explained that the committee needs at least eight members and an elected official. Commissioner Alpert moved to appoint all five (Julian "Scott" Eller, Trent Claybaugh, John Peshkin, Lori Cuson, John Simon). Motion carried 4-1, with Mayor Trice voting no. - **Historic Preservation Board (HPB)** (Item VIII.2): Vice Mayor Ohlrich moved to appoint Lorrie Muldowney to fill a vacancy. Approved unanimously (5-0). ### Unfinished Business - **Bay Park Conservancy Management and Operations Agreement** (Item IX.1): Presented by Jennifer Jorgensen and AG Lafley (CEO, BPC). The agreement consolidates usage agreements for the Chidsey Library and Municipal Auditorium into an Exhibit G to the existing partnership. Commissioners asked about rental fees, security (SPD and private), and oversight of uses (e.g., ordinances). Motion to approve carried 5-0. - **Sarasota/Manatee MPO 2026 Transportation Project Priorities List** (Item IX.2): Presented by Alvimarie Corales and Corinne Arriaga. The list includes 4 new projects (Tuttle Ave corridor, US 41 drainage, ITS/CAV tech on US 301 and Fruitville Rd). Motion to approve the list passed 5-0. A second motion to issue a letter supporting the US 41/MLK Jr. Way and US 41/Myrtle Street roundabout projects also passed 5-0. - **City Manager Search Update** (Item IX.3): City Auditor Griggs reported that 8 new applications were received over the break; the consultant’s recommendation letter expected by Wednesday, January 7. After debate on a cutoff date, the Commission voted 4-1 (Vice Mayor Ohlrich dissenting) to accept applications only until Thursday, January 8, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. The earlier motion to cutoff on Monday, January 5 died for lack of a second. Commissioners requested that the search firm provide details on sourcing and vetting of candidates. ### New Business - **Waiver of Local Preference for Downtown Master Plan Consultant** (Item XII.1): The ad-hoc committee (10-1 vote) recommended waiving the local preference provision (Procurement Code Sec. 2-368(e)) to attract the best consultant. Jennifer Jorgensen and Bill Waddill presented. Motion to approve the waiver passed 5-0. - **McCown Towers III Public Parking Discussion** (Item XII.2): A lengthy discussion on collaborating with the Sarasota Housing Authority (SHA) to add public parking spaces (two levels, 160 spaces) in the proposed senior housing development and parking garage. Broxton Harvey (Parking Manager) presented options, financial estimates ($8 million, debt service $600,000–$700,000/year), and potential metering strategies. Public speakers: Melissa Furman (opposed, citing resident quality of life), Carl Williams (Sarasota School of Arts & Sciences, supportive), David Lowe (Rosemary District resident, supportive with caution), Valerie Bouchon (McCown Towers resident, opposed on safety and security grounds), Louise Mashinist (Unitarian Universalists, echoed resident concerns), Melissa Laughlin (Rosemary District Association, supportive). Commissioners debated costs, resident concerns, and alternative parking options. A motion by Commissioner Alpert, seconded by Commissioner Battie, to direct staff to proceed with SHA to create 162 parking spaces (two levels) and return with a design addressing safety and pricing passed 4-1 (Commissioner Ahearn-Koch dissenting). The Commission also reached consensus to draft a letter supporting SHA’s Resilient SRQ application to the County Commission. - **Rescheduling March 16 Meeting** (Item XII.3): Motion to move the March 16, 2026 regular meeting to March 23, 2026. Approved 4-0 (Commissioner Battie absent during vote). ### Key Outcomes - **Approved**: DID Annual Report; ERAC Annual Report; CRA minutes; all consent items; AHAC and HPB appointments; Bay Park Management Agreement; MPO priorities list; support letters for roundabout projects; waiver of local preference for Downtown Master Plan; and rescheduling of March meeting. - **Directed**: Staff to proceed with design and pricing for two levels of public parking at McCown Towers (162 spaces) in coordination with SHA; to draft a letter supporting SHA’s Resilient SRQ application; to bring back a parking plan addressing safety and pricing. - **Set Deadline**: City manager applications accepted only until Thursday, January 8, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. - **Upcoming**: Search firm to provide recommendations by January 7; special meeting on city manager search scheduled for January 13; noise ordinance acoustic study to be initiated (budget $20,000–$25,000); staff to bring back discussion on parking code revisions.

result.title: Protecting Mother Earth: Pee'hee Mu'huh (Thacker Pass) to All Our Relations
result.creator: American Indian Airwaves
result.description: Part 1The People of the Red Mountain are an Indigenous led grassroot organization comprised of Paiute & Shoshone peoples, surrounding Indigenous nations, and supporters working to protect Pee'hee Mu'huh (Thacker Pass) from the possible construction of the Thacker Pass Lithium Mine in northwest Nevada. If the mine is built it would be the United States largest source of lithium supply generating 60,000 metric tons of battery-grade lithium carbonate annually. The People of the Red Mountain are calling for support in demanding the U.S. Department of the Interior to rescind the Thacker Pass Lithium Mine Project Final Environmental Impact Statement, Record of Decision, and Plan of Operations. Lithium Nevada Corp. is a subsidiary of the Canadian corporation Lithium Americas Corp. which proposes to build the open pit lithium mine with a project area of almost 17,933 acres that will use 5,200 acre-feet per year of water (equivalent to an average pumping rate of 3,224 gallons per minute) in one of the driest regions in the nation. Lithium Nevada Corporation characterizes the mine as a \"green\" project, despite estimates the mine will produce an estimated 152,703 tons of carbon dioxide emissions every year and will cause irreversible harm to the Fort McDermitt Paiute and Shoshone Nation, ancestral massacre sites, the water, air, medicines, culturally important wildlife relations, and everything else the land and waters culturally sustain for the Peoples. The Bureau of Land Management approved the mine on January 15, 2021, without adequately consulting our tribal members. Tune in on how support and Pee'hee Mu'huh (Thacker Pass).The People of the Red Mountain (https://peopleofredmountain.com/) are having action on April 24th, 2022, at Ildewild Park, Reno, NV from 11:00am to 5:00pm.Guests: Gary McKinney (from the Duck Valley Shoshone Paiute Nation and Fort McDermitt) of the People of the Red Mountain.Joshua Dean Sr. (Western Shoshone, Walker River Paiute Nation), of the People of the Red Mountain.Part 2:On 2/27/2022, the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group II, Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability Report was released with participation from Indigenous scholars, academics, and scientist in still a relatively new phenomenon (eight to ten years). For more sixteen years, Indigenous peoples were largely excluded in participating in the previous IPCC assessment reports. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was established by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) in 1988. In 1990, the IPCC's First Assessment Report (FAR) was published. However, in 2007, the IPCC and former U.S. President Al Gore won a Nobel Peace Prize while Indigenous peoples were absent and often locked out of the IPCC and WMO process. Today's guest is one several Indigenous academics, scholars, and scientist to participate and contribute to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group II, Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Tune in for summary and update on the report's highlight in Protecting Mother Earth. result.title: Hydatid cyst of lung: An uncommon cause of chest pain in young.
creator: Kalpana, SR
Sridhar, Kumsi
Murugan, Balaji
Moorthy, Nagaraja
Nanjappa, Manjunath C
result.description: This article is from Lung India : Official Organ of Indian Chest Society , volume 31 . Abstract Echinococcosis can involve any organ. The liver is the most common organ involved, followed by the lungs. Depending on the location of involvement it can have varied presentation. We describe a young adult presenting with chest pain secondary to a pulmonary giant hydatid cyst. A pulmonary hydatid cyst should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with chest pain without conventional risk factors of coronary artery disease, especially in a tropical region.

result.description: This article is from Indian Journal of Orthopaedics , volume 48 . Abstract Fat embolism syndrome presenting primarily with cerebral manifestations is rarely reported. We report here two such patients who showed complete recovery following initial deterioration. The importance of adequate oxygenation to prevent secondary brain damage is emphasized during prolonged recovery.

The People of the Red Mountain are calling for support in demanding the U.S. Department of the Interior to rescind the Thacker Pass Lithium Mine Project Final Environmental Impact Statement, Record of Decision, and Plan of Operations. Lithium Nevada Corp. is a subsidiary of the Canadian corporation Lithium Americas Corp. which proposes to build the open pit lithium mine with a project area of almost 17,933 acres that will use 5,200 acre-feet per year of water (equivalent to an average pumping rate of 3,224 gallons per minute) in one of the driest regions in the nation. result.title: Hot Wire 4-Axis CNC V1.0 (2834138)
result.creator: Dennis Steir (addennis)
result.description: First run video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oe-pj3NSOOw After hundreds of iterations, it's done! This is a 4-axis CNC machine that is designed to cut dynamic shapes in foam. Complex curves, letters, any shape you want. Each tower moves independently and the entire machine is adjustable to create steep angles if need be. It is built around v-slot rail, but all other parts are printable. For the most part the construction is pretty straightforward. The dimensions are totally flexible, although I've found v-slot in any length over a meter will start to twist. It requires 4 lengths of 2040; 2 the length you want horizontal travel, 2 the length you want the towers to be spaced from one another. My build supports about 44" of hotwire and is adjustable down to about 18" (for extreme angled parts). In all the pictures the machine is set to 35". For the Y & A towers, 2 lengths of 2020 are used. I'm using 1 meter lengths for these. My machine is all PETG. The build uses NEMA17 motors and GT2 timing belt. That may seem fairly weak for the sheer size of the machine, but if your wire temp and speeds are correct there will be little to no resistance. Cutting foam is more of an art than a science, so experiment with speeds and temperatures as you go. Bolts: All the axis bolts are 5mm. 55mm and 45mm lengths are required for the carriages, 12 & 16mm bolts for miscellaneous mounts and 5x30mm bolts for the belt turnarounds.You'll need a bunch of 5mm T-nuts for the v-slot mounts. I used #8 nuts and bolts for motor mounts and the carriage and belt tensioners, however, 4mm bolts are nearly identical. The motors use 3x12mm but your motors may vary. I source all my bolts from https://www.boltdepot.com/. For all hardware I used stainless steel socket cap bolts. Belts & Drive: • GT2 belts, youll need about 10 meters. • Belt Turnarounds: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01H3F8LUU/ref=oh_aui_search_detailpage?ie=UTF8&psc=1 • Timing pulley: I'm using 11-tooth but 16 will work as well depending on your microstepping: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01IMPM44O/ref=oh_aui_search_detailpage?ie=UTF8&psc=1 • Belt tensioners (I use 2 per axis): https://www.amazon.com/Mercurry-Timing-Torsion-3D-Printer/dp/B01E913IJK/ref=sr_1_cc_1?s=aps&ie=UTF8&qid=1523833455&sr=1-1-catcorr&keywords=3d+printer+timing+spring • V-slot wheels, rails can be sourced from a number of places, all 1/4" spacers I used from here: http://openbuildspartstore.com/nylon-spacers-10-pack/ • Each carriage is tensioned to the rail via adjustment_wheel.stl. Pass bolts through carriage with these on the outside; they can be turned and locked to press the wheels against the rail. Don't over-tighten. Hotwire assembly. Because the machine creates variable angles, it needs a way to keep tension on the wire with variable lengths. One side of the hot wire is anchored to the tower, the other is attached to a torsion spring. I used the entire assembly from this https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01H4E9Z6O/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o02_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1. Take it apart and use the center pulley. When you ruin the hotwire, make sure you have at least 15-20 turns around this pulley then anchor it. The hotwire passes through a welding tip screwed into Hot_Wire_Guide_Pass.stl. Welding tips available here: https://www.harborfreight.com/0025-in-mig-welding-contact-tips-10-pk-63796.html. Your hotwire supply attaches to this and passes power to the wire via contact. I have not used this extensively, so i have no idea how hot this area will get. If it overheads I'm going to build a heat-sink. Electronics: I'm using a HobbyCNC board, hence the need to use an old PC with a parallel port and Mach3. I already had the hardware but if I didn't I'd have used RAMPS. The software I'm using comes from here: http://www.profili2.com/eng/default.asp. The switch panel is designed to fit these switches: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00ZWWZ0GK/ref=oh_aui_search_detailpage?ie=UTF8&psc=1. The led strips are mounted to the towers via this: https://www.thingiverse.com/thing:2834133. The table can be made out of any 3/4" material, or v-slot. I opted to build a lighter table. Each table mount (remember to mirror 2 of them) runs a 5mm bolt through a t-nut to make the bed adjustable. Be sure to square the towers from another as well as the table. Warning: Cutting foam releases some pretty nasty stuff, make sure if you are cutting any you are in a very well ventilated area. I built a vent especially for this machine. You'll have to source your hot wire power supply. I'm not going to provide details on mine as I don't want to be liable for a fire. Be careful and have fun!

result.creator: Matt Karssen (mpkarssen)
result.description: **EDIT: I am currently waiting on PTFE Tubing, which should be here by the end of the week. I'm going to swap out the rubber grommets, which cause a little bit of drag on the filament, with the PTFE, which should be much better. I'll update with the results. I've wanted a filament enclosure for a long time. I live in a humid area, so I can only imagine how much moisture my filament is absorbing. I finally found a good box for it, and I thought I would share. Not counting shopping and printing time, the project took me about an hour and a half. 30 minutes of that was just waiting for the silicone caulking to dry. I bought everything from stores near me, but the components can easily be found online as well. I designed everything in Inventor. The dowel mounts, the grommet caps to seal the unused holes, and the dowel clips to put on either side of each spool to keep them from sliding around in the box. Check out the Imgur album for a short rundown of the whole process. http://imgur.com/a/ifo0S I bought the box from Wal-Mart for about $10, as well as a 3/8" dowel for less than $2. https://www.walmart.com/ip/Iris-Portable-File-Box-with-Organizer-Top/22374211 The rubber grommets are from my local Ace Hardware. I just asked one of the guys there who showed me their selection. I chose the smallest they had, which have a 3mm inner diameter. Something similar can also be found on Amazon, though I'd recommend checking out a hardware store first. I got mine for 23¢ each, for a total of $1.25 (including tax) https://www.amazon.com/Grooved-Blanking-Grommet-Firewall-Bushing/dp/B00P3FLVS2/ref=sr_1_3?s=hi&ie=UTF8&qid=1501004596&sr=1-3&keywords=3mm+grommet I used some silicone caulking I had laying around. Fortunately I had some left over from another project because it barely took any to line the top edge of the case. This is the kind that I had, but pretty much any silicone caulking will work: https://www.amazon.com/08641-Clear-Silicone-Sealant-9-8-Ounce/dp/B000BD0QAK/ref=sr_1_1?s=hi&ie=UTF8&qid=1501004814&sr=1-1&keywords=silicone+caulk I also designed the dowel mounts with holes for M4*5 set screws to hold the dowel in place. I just borrowed some from the spare extrusion hardware I had lying around, like this: https://www.amazon.com/Degree-Hidden-Bracket-Aluminum-Extrusion/dp/B01LWY99IT/ref=pd_sbs_60_3?_encoding=UTF8&psc=1&refRID=H9KQSKWA9MVM8AYVPMF2 I bought a 450g silica gel packet from a Scheels store near me, but they can also be found on Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/Hydrosorbent-450-Gram-Silica-Cubic/dp/B0001EJIXU/ref=sr_1_fkmr1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1501005537&sr=8-2-fkmr1&keywords=450g+silica+gel+pouch

result.title: Jacksonville City Council Meeting – May 26, 2026
result.creator: OpenPublica
result.description: # Jacksonville City Council Meeting – May 26, 2026 The Jacksonville City Council met on Tuesday, May 26, 2026, at 5:02 p.m. The meeting included an invocation, approval of minutes, a presentation honoring the restoration of the Jacob Jewelers Clock, consideration of several ordinances and resolutions, and public comment. Key actions included approval of emergency funding for a Culinary Institute of America partnership, a resolution of appreciation for retiring Council Auditor Kim Taylor, and the failure of a resolution to prohibit a new jail in historically redlined areas. ### Consent Calendar - The minutes of the May 12 regular meeting were approved. - The consent agenda (items 2026-312 through 2026-413) was approved unanimously (17-0), including the following appointments: Robin Lang (Council on Elder Affairs), Mario DeQunto (Library Board of Trustees), Ivan Mote (Downtown Development Review Board), Jeffrey Druschel (Cultural Service Grant Program Committee), Catherine Moore (Jacksonville Ethics Commission), Heather Raber and Brian Parks (Assistant Council Auditor), Kimberly Corbin (Chief of Municipal Code Compliance), Ernest Smith (Jacksonville Housing and Community Development Commission), Alice Nelson (East Side Grants Committee), Jackie B. Sheel (Civil Service Board), Raj Gupta III and Jason I. French (Jacksonville Health Facilities Authority). ### Presentations & Recognitions - **Jacob Jewelers Clock Restoration** – Councilmember Carlucci presented Resolution 2025-666 honoring Tina Savage (founder of Jack's Tours) and Alex Safakis (JWB Real Estate Companies) for restoring the iconic clock in downtown Jacksonville. The clock, one of only a few remaining in the country, had stood silent and in disrepair. Savage recognized the clock's significance during a historical walking tour and partnered with Safakis, who fully funded the restoration as a gift to the city. The resolution was adopted. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Culinary Institute of America (CIA) Partnership** – Andre Wallace (President of Jacks USA) explained that the ordinance before council set aside funds for a future redevelopment agreement with the CIA for a southeast campus in Jacksonville. He clarified that no funds would be expended until a term sheet and redevelopment agreement were approved by council. The CIA board was scheduled to vote on June 15-16 on Jacksonville as the campus location. John Nooney (District 4 resident) expressed support but called for clawback provisions and oversight. Robert Jones (Vice President of Strategic Partnerships, CIA) described the CIA's 80-year history and its impact in San Antonio, including workforce training for military and school meal programs, noting that in San Antonio the program saved the city $3 million annually by reducing school meal costs. - **Resolution on Jail Location (2026-0356)** – Multiple speakers supported the resolution to prohibit a new jail from being built in historically redlined neighborhoods. Speakers included Rev. R. LaRoy Gundy, Jaquan Easton Sr., Katie Hathaway, Lydia Bell, Isaiah Rumlin, Latavia Harris, Sally Barnes, Keanu Blaylock, Bobby O'Connor (who spoke at length about his disappointment with committee votes), Denise Scott, Etta Ettlinger, Wells Todd, Anthony Brown, Denise Cook, and others. They argued that redlining has historically harmed black communities and that a jail would further disinvest and stigmatize them. Several also criticized the city's handling of the Connor Collie case, calling the punishment disproportionate and politically motivated. - **Free to Garden Act** – Nathan Ballantyne, James Clower, Hermione Walker, and Trey Ford spoke in support of the act, which would allow market and community gardens by right in Jacksonville. Ballantyne noted that agrihoods are a growing real estate trend and that current zoning does not align with the city's comprehensive plan encouraging community gardens. Clower highlighted a Brentwood community garden that produced 2,000 pounds of food last year to address food insecurity. - **John Nooney** – Spoke on multiple public hearing items, generally raising questions about oversight, process, and the scope of various bills. He was repeatedly called to order for not speaking substantively to the bills. ### Discussion Items - **Emergency Ordinance – Culinary Institute of America (2026-0419)** – Council President Carico introduced a floor amendment with technical cleanup, including clarifying that the Tourist Development Council committed to finding other dollars within its budget rather than a direct allocation, and updating the term sheet to reflect a future allocation of city funds. The emergency was approved (16-2). Council President Carico thanked the CIA and partners, stating this could change lives in Jacksonville. - **Retirement of Council Auditor Kim Taylor (2026-0469)** – Councilmembers recognized Taylor for her 41 years of service. Dr. Johnson described her as "detailed, succinct, data-driven, informed, and wise." Council President-Elect Howland noted the city is better for her career. The resolution passed 18-0. - **Submerged Land Lease (2026-0461)** – Paul Hardin (representing Preston Hollow) requested approval of a submerged land lease amendment necessary before a state cabinet meeting in early June. The bill passed 18-0. - **Election Qualifying Deadline (2026-0474)** – A floor amendment corrected the qualifying deadline to June 12 and set the petition deadline at June 8. Supervisor of Elections Jerry Holland clarified the qualifying process. The bill passed 18-0. - **Resolution on Jail Location (2026-0356)** – Councilmember Peluso argued the resolution was a necessary guardrail to prevent building a jail in historically redlined areas, noting the council previously passed a resolution acknowledging redlining. Councilmember Salem opposed, stating the discussion should wait until a consultant's study identifies three proposed sites, and noted that remote court appearances reduce the need for a jail near the courthouse. Councilmember Diamond called the resolution "performative garbage." Councilmember Gaffney supported it, pledging to oppose a jail in his district (Northside). Councilmembers Johnson and Carlucci proposed deferral, but Peluso declined to withdraw. The resolution failed 5-12. - **Community Gardens Ordinance (2026-0362)** – The bill, which funds the CIA partnership, passed 14-1 with two abstentions (Council members declared potential conflicts due to employer ties to youth and mission services). - **Postponement of Appointment Bill (2025-0872)** – Councilmember Salem moved to postpone the bill to June 9, citing a late-arriving legal opinion from General Counsel. Council President-Elect Carlucci expressed concern about the bill's purpose and scope. The postponement passed 17-0. ### Key Outcomes - **CIA Partnership (2026-0419)** – Approved as an emergency, 16-2, after a floor amendment. - **Council Auditor Retirement (2026-0469)** – Approved 18-0. - **Submerged Land Lease (2026-0461)** – Approved 18-0. - **Election Qualifying Deadline (2026-0474)** – Approved 18-0 as amended. - **Resolution on Jail Location (2026-0356)** – Failed 5-12. - **Community Gardens Ordinance (2026-0362)** – Approved 14-1, with two abstentions. - **Appointment Bill (2025-0872)** – Postponed to June 9, 2026. - **Multiple zoning and land use items (2026-0300 through 2026-0398)** – Approved with varying votes; public hearings were closed for most items with few speakers. - **Chamber funding bills (2026-0462, 2026-0464, 2026-0465)** – Approved as emergencies, each 16-1.

result.title: Wanhao i3 mini extruder mount ( e3d v6 ) (3064171)
result.creator: Garrett Wade (Garrett_w)
result.description: This is the first version i'm going to release of this mount, I'm currently using it on my machine and have tested it on another machine so I do know that it fits. This mount was designed to properly mount the hotend, has dedicated part cooler built into it and also moves the X-axis end switch to give you more build area (this requires flashing firmware if you want to increase the build area) This was built to use m3 brass inserts for all the threads, I used ones like I used are on amazon but they can also be sourced from a number of other sources. These are easily installed by pushing them in slowly with a soldering iron. https://www.amazon.com/a16041800ux0827-Cylindrical-Knurled-Threaded-Embedded/dp/B01IZ1RN0A/ref=sr_1_6?s=industrial&ie=UTF8&qid=1535055018&sr=1-6&keywords=m3+brass+insert I took the original hot end fan and mounted it to the fan duct built into this design, and added a 30mm fan to cool the hot end like the original e3d hotend ships with. E3D V6 fans and ducts or copies can be purchased for very cheap online. Due to the new position of the X-axis endstop you may need to push LM8UU X-axis bearings over towards the left (X axis max position) to ensure they do not hit and allow the machine home. The bearings are firmly held in place but should push over without too much difficulty I will probably refine this design later when I get more time and post updates to it.

result.title: Identifying stable hotspots and coldspots in firearm homicide across the US during a period of nationally increasing trends, 2014 to 2022
creator: Michelle Degli Esposti
Ali Rowhani-Rahbar
Douglas Wiebe
Elinore Kaufman
result.description: Background Firearm violence is the leading cause of premature death in the United States.1,2 In 2021, firearms caused nearly 49,000 fatalities – the highest number of deaths on record – of which a growing proportion are firearm homicides.3,4 Despite decreases in the 1990s and early 2000s, firearm homicide has increased in recent years, with 2014 marking a year of changing trends. The first year of the COVID-19 pandemic (2020) further marked a period of unprecedented increases in firearm homicide.5–8 While firearm violence is now widely acknowledged to be an urgent public health problem,9–11 syndromic surveillance and epidemiological methods used to prevent other critical diseases are still under-utilized in firearm research.12–14 Spatial and temporal scan statistics are a powerful epidemiological tool used to detect clusters which show disproportionately high (or low) incidences of a disease (i.e., hotspots, or coldspots).14,15 Used prospectively, the method enables disease surveillance in real-time and the early detection of disease outbreaks.16 When used retrospectively, scan statistics can evaluate geographical variation over any time period, including identifying spatial clusters – hotspots and coldspots – and the time period these areas showed an “unusual” excess (or lack) of observed incidences.17 The systematic study of geographical variation is critical for guiding targeted interventions, anticipating need and facilitating the effective delivery of health-related services.15 In addition, understanding spatio-temporal patterns sheds key insights into how demographic, social, cultural, and environmental factors may be influencing morbidity and mortality. Previous firearm research has demonstrated the importance of these exploratory spatio-temporal analyses in assisting inductive research and generating hypotheses for explaining changes in firearm violence over time.17–19 While recent studies have highlighted geographical differences in firearm homicide across US states and counties,3,5,18–21 the stability of hotspots and coldspots over time is poorly understood. Specifically, it is unclear whether recent rises in firearm homicide since 2014 are primarily accounted for by increasing trends in the same localities that have historically borne a disproportionate burden of firearm violence or, whether recent years, including COVID-19 years, showed different spatio-temporal clustering giving rise to new hotspots and/or coldspots across the US. Understanding emerging geographical patterns in firearm homicide is not only essential to inform and update service provision but will also point towards potential explanations for the unprecedented rise in firearm homicide since 2014. For example, the detection of hotspots primarily in areas that experienced high-profile incidents of police brutality against Black men, such as the killing of Michael Brown in Fergusson, Missouri, would lend support for the Fergusson effect,6,22 whereas evidence of hotspots in areas that experienced a high toll of COVID-19 deaths would lend support for the role of the pandemic in driving recent increases in firearm homicide.23 In this proposed study, we will advance the evidence by applying space-time scan statistics14 – a powerful epidemiological tool15,16 – to systematically analyze spatio-temporal variation in firearm homicide from 2014 to 2022. We will use restricted access yearly mortality data at the county-level to identify stable hotspots and coldspots during the years in which firearm homicide showed national increases before (2014-2019) and during (2020-2022) the COVID-19 pandemic. We will also investigate spatial variation in temporal trends during these two time periods to generate exploratory evidence for possible explanations to why firearm homicide has, on average, increased in the US since 2014. Methods The proposed study will be a descriptive cross-sectional analysis which uses yearly firearm homicide data in all counties that form part of contiguous United States (i.e., 48 states and the District of Columbia) from January 2014 to December 2022. In addition to excluding Alaska and Hawaii, we will exclude any counties that experienced definitional changes during the study period.24 While our study period will span from 2014 to 2022, we will analyze two time periods separately: the years of national increase before COVID-19 (2014-2019) and the years during and after the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2022). We will follow recommendations set out in the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline. Because the data source is publicly available and the data are anonymous, the study will be exempt from the need for informed consent in accordance with 45 CFR §46.102(f). The study has been approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board (HUM00246835). References 1. Goldstick JE, Cunningham RM, Carter PM. result.creator: theRSA.org
result.description: Accelerating the pace of change Join us in London, Osaka and online for the second event in our global partnership with the UK at Expo 2025. 5 August 2025, 09.30-10.30 (London) 17.30-18.30 (Osaka). Join us from 8:30 to 9:30am for networking over tea, coffee, and pastries at RSA House, ahead of the live simulcast panel. A chance to connect with speakers, delegates, and colleagues working across gender equity and policy. The UK has a rich history of advancing women’s rights. In 1918, the Representation of the People Act granted voting rights to women over 30, with equal suffrage achieved in 1928. From the Equal Pay Act of 1970 to the Equality Act of 2010, trailblazing women have been at the forefront of building collective movements for progress and justice. But there remain stubborn challenges and barriers to women’s full economic, legal, and social empowerment. Linking speakers in the historic Great Room of the RSA in London and in the UK Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka, this event will hear from today’s disruptors, influencers and innovators leading the charge for the protection and advancement of the rights of women and girls in the UK, and internationally – and for a future where everyone has equal opportunity to achieve their full potential. More speakers will be announced soon. Speakers: Penny East, Chief Executive at the Fawcett Society Sakshi Bansal, Founder of Project Leap, Sr. Advisor at Private Equity Investments (Arup, UK), and President (SDGs) of the Women’s Chamber of Commerce (New Delhi, India) Chika Sudo, Head of Arts at the British Council in Japan Chairs: Nina Nannar, journalist and arts editor for ITV News (London) Carolyn Davidson, UK Commissioner General for Expo 2025 (Osaka) RSA and UK at Expo 2025 Osaka, Kansai A bold new events partnership celebrating the UK as a place to come to study, visit and invest, and as a country of innovation and creativity where the world can come to build the future. With the deadline to the UN’s 2030 Sustainable Development Goals just five years away, the RSA and UK at Expo 2025 partnership will tackle global issues from inequality to climate change, exploring the progress that has been made and the work still to be done to secure health and wellbeing, peace, justice, and prosperity for communities worldwide.
